questions.explanation: TNF and IL-1 activate endothelium and promote cytokine/chemokine cascades; systemically, they also contribute to fever.

questions.prompt: Which complement fragment is both a potent chemoattractant and an anaphylatoxin?
questions.explanation: C5a recruits and activates leukocytes and also increases vascular permeability through mast cell activation.

questions.prompt: Which complement component is the major opsonin generated during complement activation?
questions.explanation: C3b coats microbes and promotes phagocytosis through complement receptors.

questions.topic: Introduction, Causes, and Recognition of Inflammation
questions.prompt: Which pair of tissue components carries out the two major reactions of inflammation?
questions.explanation: Inflammation depends chiefly on vascular reactions and leukocyte responses, which together deliver plasma proteins and effector cells to the site of injury.

questions.topic: Introduction, Causes, and Recognition of Inflammation
questions.prompt: Why can inflammation itself become harmful?
options: Leukocyte products and mediators can injure normal host tissues
It blocks all plasma proteins from leaving vessels
It permanently prevents immunity against microbes
questions.answer: Leukocyte products and mediators can injure normal host tissues
questions.explanation: The same enzymes, ROS, cytokines, and mediators that attack microbes can damage bystander tissues when excessive or misdirected.

questions.topic: Introduction, Causes, and Recognition of Inflammation
questions.prompt: Which set contains the classic local signs of acute inflammation described in pathology?
questions.explanation: Redness, heat, swelling, and pain reflect vasodilation, vascular leakage, and mediator effects on nerves.

questions.topic: Introduction, Causes, and Recognition of Inflammation
questions.prompt: What is the main protective purpose of inflammation?
options: To wall off every wound permanently with collagen
To prevent all leukocytes from entering tissue
To eliminate the offending agent and initiate repair
To replace the immune system with coagulation
questions.answer: To eliminate the offending agent and initiate repair
questions.explanation: Inflammation removes microbes or damaged tissue and sets the stage for tissue repair.

questions.topic: Introduction, Causes, and Recognition of Inflammation
questions.prompt: Which description best defines acute inflammation?
options: Slow mononuclear infiltrate with fibrosis as the initial event
Pure lymphocyte proliferation without vascular changes
Permanent scar formation without mediator release
Rapid response with vascular leakage and predominantly neutrophilic infiltrate
questions.answer: Rapid response with vascular leakage and predominantly neutrophilic infiltrate
questions.explanation: Acute inflammation begins quickly, is usually short-lived, and commonly features edema and neutrophils.

questions.topic: Introduction, Causes, and Recognition of Inflammation
questions.prompt: Which description best defines chronic inflammation?
options: Prolonged inflammation with mononuclear cells, tissue destruction, and repair
A brief neutrophil-rich response lasting minutes
A response limited to histamine release from mast cells
A nonvascular response without leukocyte recruitment
questions.answer: Prolonged inflammation with mononuclear cells, tissue destruction, and repair
questions.explanation: Chronic inflammation combines continuing injury, macrophages/lymphocytes, tissue damage, and attempts at healing.

questions.topic: Introduction, Causes, and Recognition of Inflammation
questions.prompt: A sterile focus of necrotic tissue releases ATP, uric acid, and DNA fragments. These molecules are best classified as:
questions.explanation: Endogenous products of injured or necrotic cells act as DAMPs that trigger inflammation even without infection.

questions.topic: Introduction, Causes, and Recognition of Inflammation
questions.prompt: Toll-like receptors are especially important in inflammation because they:
options: Recognize conserved microbial products and activate inflammatory signaling
questions.answer: Recognize conserved microbial products and activate inflammatory signaling
questions.explanation: TLRs are pattern-recognition receptors that detect microbial PAMPs and stimulate cytokine and inflammatory responses.

questions.topic: Introduction, Causes, and Recognition of Inflammation
questions.prompt: Activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome most directly promotes inflammation by increasing production of:
questions.explanation: The inflammasome activates caspase-1, which converts pro-IL-1 beta into active IL-1, a potent inflammatory cytokine.

questions.topic: Introduction, Causes, and Recognition of Inflammation
questions.prompt: Which stimulus is a typical trigger for inflammation through recognition of microbial or damaged-cell products?
questions.explanation: Microbial products such as LPS are PAMPs recognized by innate immune receptors.

questions.topic: Morphologic Patterns and Outcomes of Acute Inflammation
questions.prompt: Serous inflammation is characterized by:
options: Thick pus with liquefactive necrosis only
questions.explanation: Serous inflammation produces watery effusions or blisters derived from plasma or mesothelial secretions.

questions.topic: Morphologic Patterns and Outcomes of Acute Inflammation
questions.prompt: The three core events in acute inflammation are best summarized as:
options: Vascular changes, leukocyte recruitment/activation, and mediator action
questions.answer: Vascular changes, leukocyte recruitment/activation, and mediator action
questions.explanation: Acute inflammation is driven by vascular responses, leukocyte movement and activation, and chemical mediators.

questions.topic: Morphologic Patterns and Outcomes of Acute Inflammation
questions.prompt: Fibrinous inflammation most often indicates:
options: More severe vascular leakage with fibrinogen escape
questions.answer: More severe vascular leakage with fibrinogen escape
questions.explanation: When vascular permeability is high, fibrinogen leaks out and is converted to fibrin.

questions.topic: Morphologic Patterns and Outcomes of Acute Inflammation
questions.prompt: Purulent or suppurative inflammation is characterized by:
options: Pus rich in neutrophils and liquefactive debris
questions.answer: Pus rich in neutrophils and liquefactive debris
questions.explanation: Suppurative inflammation contains neutrophils, necrotic debris, and edema fluid.

questions.topic: Morphologic Patterns and Outcomes of Acute Inflammation
questions.prompt: An abscess is best described as:
options: A localized collection of pus in tissue
A sterile transudate in a serous cavity
questions.answer: A localized collection of pus in tissue
questions.explanation: Abscesses are focal suppurative lesions with central liquefactive necrosis and many neutrophils.

questions.topic: Morphologic Patterns and Outcomes of Acute Inflammation
questions.prompt: An ulcer is:
options: A granuloma made entirely of macrophages
A local defect of an epithelial surface produced by shedding necrotic inflamed tissue
A vascular dilation without tissue loss
questions.answer: A local defect of an epithelial surface produced by shedding necrotic inflamed tissue
questions.explanation: Ulcers occur on skin or mucosal surfaces when necrotic inflammatory tissue is lost.

questions.topic: Morphologic Patterns and Outcomes of Acute Inflammation
questions.prompt: Complete resolution of acute inflammation is most likely when:
options: Injury is limited, short-lived, and tissue can regenerate
Large amounts of fibrin cannot be cleared
questions.answer: Injury is limited, short-lived, and tissue can regenerate
questions.explanation: Resolution requires removal of mediators/debris and preservation of regenerative capacity and tissue framework.

questions.topic: Morphologic Patterns and Outcomes of Acute Inflammation
questions.prompt: Organization and scarring are favored when:
options: The injury is tiny and the matrix is intact
The tissue has no vascular leakage
There is substantial tissue destruction or abundant fibrinous exudate
questions.answer: There is substantial tissue destruction or abundant fibrinous exudate
questions.explanation: If exudate or necrotic tissue cannot be cleared, granulation tissue grows into it and collagen scar forms.

questions.topic: Morphologic Patterns and Outcomes of Acute Inflammation
questions.prompt: Progression from acute to chronic inflammation is most likely when:
options: The injurious agent persists or normal healing is interfered with
Neutrophils undergo prompt apoptosis and macrophages clear debris
The basement membrane is intact and injury is trivial
questions.answer: The injurious agent persists or normal healing is interfered with
questions.explanation: Persistent infection, foreign material, autoimmune injury, or delayed clearance can convert acute inflammation into chronic inflammation.

questions.topic: Morphologic Patterns and Outcomes of Acute Inflammation
questions.prompt: A fibrinous pericarditis can either resolve or become organized. Organization means:
options: Immediate conversion of fibrin into normal mesothelium
Ingrowth of fibroblasts and vessels followed by scar formation
Loss of all inflammatory cells without repair
Transformation of fibrin into red blood cells
questions.answer: Ingrowth of fibroblasts and vessels followed by scar formation
questions.explanation: Organization is replacement of fibrinous exudate by granulation tissue and eventually fibrous scar.

questions.prompt: Tissue repair occurs by which two broad processes?
questions.explanation: Repair restores tissue by regenerating cells and/or forming scar through connective tissue deposition.

questions.prompt: During scar maturation, early type III collagen is gradually replaced mainly by:
questions.explanation: Healing scars become stronger as type I collagen replaces the initially deposited type III collagen.

questions.prompt: Labile cells are cells that:
questions.explanation: Labile tissues, such as epithelia and hematopoietic cells, have continuous cell turnover.

questions.prompt: Permanent cells are best exemplified by:
questions.explanation: Permanent cells have little or no proliferative ability, so injury usually heals by scar.

questions.prompt: Why is an intact extracellular matrix important for regeneration?
options: It blocks all growth factor signaling
It converts all cells into fibroblasts
It preserves the scaffold needed for orderly cell growth
questions.answer: It preserves the scaffold needed for orderly cell growth
questions.explanation: Regeneration needs an intact stromal framework; ECM destruction favors scarring.

questions.prompt: Liver regeneration after partial hepatectomy is mainly achieved by:
options: Proliferation of remaining hepatocytes and nonparenchymal cells
questions.answer: Proliferation of remaining hepatocytes and nonparenchymal cells
questions.explanation: The liver can restore mass through cytokine priming and growth factor-driven proliferation of residual cells.

questions.prompt: Granulation tissue is composed mainly of:
options: Only mature dense collagen without vessels
New vessels, proliferating fibroblasts, and loose extracellular matrix
questions.answer: New vessels, proliferating fibroblasts, and loose extracellular matrix
questions.explanation: Granulation tissue is a vascular, fibroblast-rich provisional repair tissue.

questions.prompt: Which growth factor is most important in angiogenesis during repair?
questions.explanation: VEGF stimulates endothelial migration, proliferation, and new vessel formation.

questions.prompt: The most important fibrogenic cytokine in scar formation is:
questions.explanation: TGF-beta increases collagen synthesis, decreases collagen degradation, and promotes fibroblast activity.

questions.prompt: Matrix metalloproteinases in healing wounds are important because they:
options: Remodel extracellular matrix and are balanced by TIMPs
Serve as the main opsonins for bacteria
questions.answer: Remodel extracellular matrix and are balanced by TIMPs
questions.explanation: MMPs degrade matrix components during remodeling, while tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases limit their activity.

questions.prompt: The acute-phase response is driven mainly by which cytokines?
questions.explanation: TNF, IL-1, and especially IL-6 mediate many systemic responses to inflammation.

questions.prompt: A leukemoid reaction is best described as:
options: Extreme reactive leukocytosis that can mimic leukemia
questions.answer: Extreme reactive leukocytosis that can mimic leukemia
questions.explanation: Severe infections can produce very high leukocyte counts, sometimes 40,000 to 100,000 per microliter, mimicking leukemia.

questions.prompt: Fever in inflammation occurs because cytokines induce hypothalamic production of:
questions.explanation: IL-1 and TNF stimulate prostaglandin production in the hypothalamus, raising the temperature set point.

questions.prompt: Which set contains important acute-phase proteins?
options: C-reactive protein, fibrinogen, and serum amyloid A
questions.answer: C-reactive protein, fibrinogen, and serum amyloid A
questions.explanation: The liver increases synthesis of CRP, fibrinogen, and SAA during systemic inflammation.

questions.prompt: In many bacterial infections, leukocytosis is dominated by:
questions.explanation: Bacterial infections commonly cause increased circulating neutrophils.

questions.prompt: A left shift in acute inflammation means increased circulating:
options: Immature neutrophils such as band forms
questions.answer: Immature neutrophils such as band forms
questions.explanation: Accelerated marrow release during inflammation increases immature granulocyte forms in blood.

questions.prompt: Fibrinogen increases the erythrocyte sedimentation rate by promoting:
questions.explanation: Fibrinogen coats red cells, making them stack and sediment faster.

questions.prompt: CRP and serum amyloid A can help host defense by:
options: Binding microbes and acting as opsonins or complement activators
questions.answer: Binding microbes and acting as opsonins or complement activators
questions.explanation: CRP and SAA bind microbial components and damaged cells, enhancing clearance.

questions.prompt: High, sustained TNF production in chronic inflammation contributes to:
questions.explanation: TNF suppresses appetite and alters metabolism, contributing to wasting/cachexia.

questions.prompt: Septic shock reflects excessive systemic inflammatory mediator release causing:
options: Pure collagen scar without vascular effects
Hypotension, disseminated coagulation, and metabolic abnormalities
questions.answer: Hypotension, disseminated coagulation, and metabolic abnormalities
questions.explanation: Systemic cytokine excess in sepsis can cause vasodilation, vascular leakage, DIC, and multiorgan failure.

questions.prompt: Redness and warmth in acute inflammation are mainly caused by:
questions.explanation: Arteriolar vasodilation increases local blood flow, producing rubor and calor.

questions.prompt: Which plasma protein entering an inflamed site can form a fibrinous mesh when vascular permeability is high?
questions.explanation: Leaked fibrinogen can be converted to fibrin, especially in severe vascular injury or leakage.

questions.prompt: An exudate differs from a transudate because an exudate is:
options: Protein-poor and caused only by hydrostatic pressure
Protein-rich and caused by increased vascular permeability
questions.answer: Protein-rich and caused by increased vascular permeability
questions.explanation: Inflammatory endothelial leakage produces protein-rich fluid and often cells, whereas transudates are low-protein ultrafiltrates.

questions.prompt: Edema means:
options: Loss of tissue fluid from dehydration
Excess fluid in interstitial tissue or serous cavities
questions.answer: Excess fluid in interstitial tissue or serous cavities
questions.explanation: Edema is abnormal fluid accumulation in tissues or body cavities.

questions.prompt: The most common mechanism of vascular leakage in acute inflammation is:
options: Complete arterial rupture in every case
questions.explanation: Histamine, bradykinin, and leukotrienes commonly cause endothelial contraction and intercellular gaps in venules.

questions.prompt: Which mediator is classically linked to rapid, transient endothelial contraction and vascular leakage?
questions.explanation: Histamine from mast cells is a classic early mediator of venular leakage.

questions.prompt: Stasis in acute inflammation develops mainly because:
options: Fluid leaves vessels, concentrating red cells and slowing flow
Endothelium stops expressing all adhesion molecules
questions.answer: Fluid leaves vessels, concentrating red cells and slowing flow
questions.explanation: Loss of plasma fluid increases blood viscosity, producing slower flow and leukocyte margination.

questions.prompt: What is the role of lymphatic vessels during acute inflammation?
options: Produce all neutrophils in the lesion
Prevent any antigen from reaching lymph nodes
Drain extravascular fluid, proteins, and leukocytes from the site
questions.answer: Drain extravascular fluid, proteins, and leukocytes from the site
questions.explanation: Lymphatics help clear edema and inflammatory cells; inflamed lymphatics or nodes may cause lymphangitis or lymphadenitis.

questions.prompt: A severe burn directly damages endothelium, causing leakage that persists until repair occurs. This is best explained by:
options: Selective loss of oncotic pressure without injury
questions.explanation: Endothelial necrosis or detachment causes sustained leakage because the vascular barrier is physically disrupted.

questions.prompt: VEGF promotes inflammation-associated edema primarily by:
options: Increasing vascular permeability and endothelial responses
questions.answer: Increasing vascular permeability and endothelial responses
questions.explanation: VEGF is a potent inducer of vascular permeability and also supports new vessel growth during repair.

questions.topic: Cutaneous Wound Healing and Pathologic Repair
questions.prompt: Healing by first intention occurs in:
options: A large infected ulcer with extensive tissue loss
A clean, sutured surgical incision with minimal tissue loss
A burn wound healing entirely by contraction
questions.answer: A clean, sutured surgical incision with minimal tissue loss
questions.explanation: Primary union is typical of clean incised wounds with closely apposed edges.

questions.topic: Cutaneous Wound Healing and Pathologic Repair
questions.prompt: Fibrosis in parenchymal organs most often follows:
options: A single trivial injury with intact matrix and rapid resolution
Chronic inflammation with persistent injury and repair signaling
questions.answer: Chronic inflammation with persistent injury and repair signaling
questions.explanation: Persistent injury activates macrophages and fibroblasts, causing excessive extracellular matrix deposition and organ fibrosis.

questions.topic: Cutaneous Wound Healing and Pathologic Repair
questions.prompt: Healing by second intention is characterized by:
options: Larger tissue defects with more inflammation, granulation tissue, and contraction
Instant restoration of normal tissue strength
questions.answer: Larger tissue defects with more inflammation, granulation tissue, and contraction
questions.explanation: Secondary union occurs when wounds have substantial tissue loss or separated edges.

questions.topic: Cutaneous Wound Healing and Pathologic Repair
questions.prompt: Wound contraction is mediated mainly by:
questions.explanation: Myofibroblasts have contractile features that pull wound edges together.

questions.topic: Cutaneous Wound Healing and Pathologic Repair
questions.prompt: The most important local cause of delayed wound healing is:
questions.explanation: Infection prolongs inflammation and increases local tissue injury, strongly delaying repair.

questions.topic: Cutaneous Wound Healing and Pathologic Repair
questions.prompt: Which systemic factor impairs wound healing?
questions.explanation: Diabetes impairs perfusion, leukocyte function, and matrix production, delaying repair.

questions.topic: Cutaneous Wound Healing and Pathologic Repair
questions.prompt: Tensile strength of a skin wound after healing usually reaches:
options: About 70% to 80% of normal skin at maximum
questions.answer: About 70% to 80% of normal skin at maximum
questions.explanation: Wound strength rises over months but generally plateaus below normal unwounded skin strength.

questions.topic: Cutaneous Wound Healing and Pathologic Repair
questions.prompt: A keloid differs from a hypertrophic scar because a keloid:
options: Extends beyond the boundaries of the original wound
questions.answer: Extends beyond the boundaries of the original wound
questions.explanation: Keloids are exuberant scars that grow beyond the original wound margins; hypertrophic scars remain confined.

questions.topic: Cutaneous Wound Healing and Pathologic Repair
questions.prompt: Wound dehiscence is especially likely after abdominal surgery when poor healing combines with:
options: Increased mechanical stress such as coughing or vomiting
questions.answer: Increased mechanical stress such as coughing or vomiting
questions.explanation: Mechanical stress on a weak healing wound can cause the wound edges to separate.

questions.topic: Cutaneous Wound Healing and Pathologic Repair
questions.prompt: Contractures are pathologic because they:
options: Cause deformity by excessive wound contraction
questions.answer: Cause deformity by excessive wound contraction
questions.explanation: Excessive contraction can limit movement and deform tissues, especially after burns or wounds over joints.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Defects of primary hemostasis most often cause:
questions.explanation: Platelet/vWF problems commonly present with skin and mucosal bleeding.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Chronic external blood loss most characteristically causes:
questions.explanation: Repeated loss of red cells and iron, such as GI or menstrual bleeding, depletes iron stores.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Defects of secondary hemostasis most often cause:
options: Deep soft tissue bleeding and hemarthroses
questions.answer: Deep soft tissue bleeding and hemarthroses
questions.explanation: Coagulation factor deficiencies tend to cause deeper bleeding into muscles and joints.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Hemarthrosis is especially characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Severe factor VIII or IX deficiency classically causes recurrent joint bleeding.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: A patient with thrombocytopenia is at particular risk for:
options: Petechiae and potentially fatal intracerebral hemorrhage
questions.answer: Petechiae and potentially fatal intracerebral hemorrhage
questions.explanation: Very low platelet counts impair primary hemostasis and can cause serious bleeding.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Aspirin can produce a mild bleeding tendency because it:
questions.explanation: Platelets cannot resynthesize cyclooxygenase, so aspirin reduces platelet aggregation.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Uremia causes bleeding mainly by:
questions.explanation: Renal failure can impair platelet function and primary hemostasis.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Scurvy may cause purpura and ecchymoses because:
options: Defective collagen weakens small vessel walls
questions.answer: Defective collagen weakens small vessel walls
questions.explanation: Vitamin C deficiency impairs collagen synthesis, increasing vascular fragility.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Palpable purpura most strongly suggests:
options: Small-vessel inflammation or vascular wall injury
questions.answer: Small-vessel inflammation or vascular wall injury
questions.explanation: Vasculitis and vessel wall disorders can cause palpable purpuric lesions.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Rapid loss of more than about 20% of blood volume can lead to:
questions.explanation: Large acute blood loss reduces effective circulating volume and tissue perfusion.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.topic: Platelets, Coagulation Factors, and Anticoagulant Mechanisms
questions.prompt: The prothrombin time primarily screens the:
questions.explanation: PT assesses factors VII, X, V, II, and fibrinogen.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.topic: Platelets, Coagulation Factors, and Anticoagulant Mechanisms
questions.prompt: Tissue factor pathway inhibitor limits coagulation by inhibiting:
questions.explanation: TFPI restrains the tissue factor pathway, helping confine coagulation to the injury site.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.topic: Platelets, Coagulation Factors, and Anticoagulant Mechanisms
questions.prompt: The partial thromboplastin time primarily screens the:
questions.explanation: PTT assesses factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II, and fibrinogen.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.topic: Platelets, Coagulation Factors, and Anticoagulant Mechanisms
questions.prompt: Vitamin K is needed for gamma-carboxylation of:
options: Factors I, V, VIII, and XIII only
Factors II, VII, IX, and X
questions.answer: Factors II, VII, IX, and X
questions.explanation: Vitamin K-dependent carboxylation allows calcium binding by several coagulation factors.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.topic: Platelets, Coagulation Factors, and Anticoagulant Mechanisms
questions.prompt: The most important in vivo initiator of coagulation after injury is:
questions.explanation: Tissue factor exposed or expressed at injury sites complexes with VIIa to initiate coagulation.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.topic: Platelets, Coagulation Factors, and Anticoagulant Mechanisms
questions.prompt: Plasmin limits clot size by:
questions.explanation: Plasmin is the major fibrinolytic enzyme and breaks down fibrin polymers.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.topic: Platelets, Coagulation Factors, and Anticoagulant Mechanisms
questions.prompt: Tissue plasminogen activator acts by:
questions.explanation: t-PA promotes fibrinolysis by generating plasmin.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.topic: Platelets, Coagulation Factors, and Anticoagulant Mechanisms
questions.prompt: Antithrombin inhibits thrombin and several clotting factors, and its activity is enhanced by:
questions.explanation: Heparin accelerates antithrombin activity against thrombin and factors including Xa.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.topic: Platelets, Coagulation Factors, and Anticoagulant Mechanisms
questions.prompt: Thrombomodulin on intact endothelium changes thrombin activity by:
questions.explanation: Thrombin bound to thrombomodulin activates protein C, which inhibits Va and VIIIa with protein S.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.topic: Platelets, Coagulation Factors, and Anticoagulant Mechanisms
questions.prompt: Activated protein C with protein S inhibits:
questions.explanation: The protein C/S system is an endothelial anticoagulant mechanism that turns off key cofactors.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Hyperemia is:
options: A passive process from impaired venous outflow
An active process caused by arteriolar dilation and increased inflow
questions.answer: An active process caused by arteriolar dilation and increased inflow
questions.explanation: Hyperemia is active vascular dilation, such as in exercise or inflammation.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Why can a small intracranial hemorrhage be fatal while a larger subcutaneous hemorrhage may not be?
options: The rigid skull permits pressure rise and compression of vital brain tissue
questions.answer: The rigid skull permits pressure rise and compression of vital brain tissue
questions.explanation: Location matters; intracranial bleeding can raise pressure and cause herniation or perfusion failure.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Congestion is:
options: A passive process caused by impaired venous outflow
questions.answer: A passive process caused by impaired venous outflow
questions.explanation: Congestion results from venous obstruction or heart failure and produces cyanotic, blood-filled tissues.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Petechiae are best described as:
questions.explanation: Petechiae are tiny hemorrhages often linked to platelet defects or thrombocytopenia.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Chronic passive congestion of the lung commonly produces:
questions.explanation: Repeated capillary rupture in congested lungs leaves iron pigment in macrophages.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: A nutmeg liver is associated with:
questions.explanation: Right-sided heart failure can cause centrilobular congestion and a mottled liver appearance.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Purpura are larger than petechiae and measure at least about:
questions.explanation: Purpura are hemorrhages larger than petechiae; ecchymoses are larger bruises.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Ecchymoses are commonly called:
questions.explanation: Ecchymoses are larger subcutaneous hemorrhages, typically 1 to 2 cm.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: The color change in an old bruise from blue-red to green-brown mainly reflects:
options: Hemoglobin breakdown and hemosiderin/bilirubin pigment formation
questions.answer: Hemoglobin breakdown and hemosiderin/bilirubin pigment formation
questions.explanation: Extravasated red cells are degraded, generating pigments that alter the bruise color.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: A hematoma is:
options: A localized mass of extravasated blood
questions.answer: A localized mass of extravasated blood
questions.explanation: A hematoma is blood accumulated within tissues, sometimes forming a palpable mass.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Edema is best defined as:
options: Excess fluid in interstitial tissues or serous cavities
questions.answer: Excess fluid in interstitial tissues or serous cavities
questions.explanation: Edema is abnormal fluid accumulation outside vascular spaces, either in tissues or body cavities.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Which combination most strongly favors transudative edema?
options: Increased hydrostatic pressure with reduced plasma oncotic pressure
questions.answer: Increased hydrostatic pressure with reduced plasma oncotic pressure
questions.explanation: Transudates reflect pressure imbalance, particularly elevated hydrostatic or decreased oncotic pressure.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: A transudate is typically:
options: Protein-poor fluid caused by hydrostatic or oncotic imbalance
A clot made of platelets and fibrin
A collection of neutrophils and necrotic debris
questions.answer: Protein-poor fluid caused by hydrostatic or oncotic imbalance
questions.explanation: Transudates arise from noninflammatory pressure changes and have low protein and few cells.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: An exudate is usually produced by:
questions.explanation: Inflammatory endothelial leakage permits proteins and cells to enter extravascular spaces.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Generalized edema due to congestive heart failure is mainly driven by:
questions.explanation: Venous congestion increases hydrostatic pressure, pushing fluid out of vessels.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Nephrotic syndrome causes edema primarily through:
options: Reduced plasma oncotic pressure from albumin loss
questions.answer: Reduced plasma oncotic pressure from albumin loss
questions.explanation: Heavy proteinuria lowers plasma albumin and oncotic pressure, favoring fluid movement into tissues.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Lymphatic obstruction causes edema because it:
options: Prevents removal of interstitial fluid and proteins
questions.answer: Prevents removal of interstitial fluid and proteins
questions.explanation: Blocked lymphatics impair return of extravascular fluid and proteins to the circulation.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Pulmonary edema is clinically dangerous because it can:
options: Impair gas exchange in alveolar spaces
Convert red infarcts into white infarcts
questions.answer: Impair gas exchange in alveolar spaces
questions.explanation: Fluid in alveoli increases diffusion distance and can cause hypoxemia.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Pitting edema occurs when pressure on swollen subcutaneous tissue:
options: Displaces interstitial fluid and leaves a temporary depression
questions.answer: Displaces interstitial fluid and leaves a temporary depression
questions.explanation: Mobile interstitial fluid can be pushed aside, creating a transient pit.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Brain edema is especially dangerous because:
options: The skull limits expansion and raised pressure can compromise perfusion or cause herniation
Brain tissue has abundant collateral lymphatics
It always remains limited to subcutaneous tissue
questions.answer: The skull limits expansion and raised pressure can compromise perfusion or cause herniation
questions.explanation: Intracranial swelling in a closed space can raise pressure and injure vital centers.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: An embolus is:
options: A fixed bruise in subcutaneous tissue
A detached intravascular solid, liquid, or gas mass carried by blood
questions.answer: A detached intravascular solid, liquid, or gas mass carried by blood
questions.explanation: Emboli travel through blood and lodge at distant sites.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Amniotic fluid embolism is dangerous because it can cause:
options: Sudden respiratory distress, shock, seizures, and DIC
questions.answer: Sudden respiratory distress, shock, seizures, and DIC
questions.explanation: Entry of amniotic fluid into maternal circulation can trigger pulmonary dysfunction, shock, and consumptive coagulopathy.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Most pulmonary emboli arise from:
options: Deep veins of the lower limbs
questions.answer: Deep veins of the lower limbs
questions.explanation: Deep venous thrombi are the common source of pulmonary thromboembolism.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Systemic arterial emboli most commonly lodge in:
questions.explanation: Systemic emboli travel through arterial circulation and often affect legs, brain, bowel, kidney, or spleen.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: A saddle pulmonary embolus lodges at:
options: The bifurcation of the main pulmonary artery
questions.answer: The bifurcation of the main pulmonary artery
questions.explanation: Large emboli can straddle the pulmonary artery bifurcation and cause sudden death.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Small recurrent pulmonary emboli may cause:
questions.explanation: Repeated embolic obstruction can increase pulmonary vascular resistance.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Fat embolism syndrome classically follows:
options: Long bone fractures or soft tissue trauma
questions.answer: Long bone fractures or soft tissue trauma
questions.explanation: Marrow fat can enter torn vessels after skeletal trauma.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: The classic triad of fat embolism syndrome includes respiratory distress, neurologic symptoms, and:
questions.explanation: Fat embolism syndrome presents with pulmonary insufficiency, neurologic signs, anemia/thrombocytopenia, and petechiae.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Air embolism in divers is related to:
options: Gas bubbles coming out of solution during rapid decompression
questions.answer: Gas bubbles coming out of solution during rapid decompression
questions.explanation: Decompression can form nitrogen bubbles that obstruct vessels and injure tissue.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Caisson disease is another name for:
questions.explanation: Caisson disease occurs when dissolved gases form bubbles during decompression.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.topic: Fate and Clinical Consequences of Thrombi, including DIC
questions.prompt: Propagation of a thrombus means:
options: Accumulation of more platelets and fibrin
questions.answer: Accumulation of more platelets and fibrin
questions.explanation: A thrombus may enlarge by additional platelet and fibrin deposition.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.topic: Fate and Clinical Consequences of Thrombi, including DIC
questions.prompt: Bleeding in DIC occurs mainly because:
options: Platelets and coagulation factors are consumed and fibrinolysis is activated
questions.answer: Platelets and coagulation factors are consumed and fibrinolysis is activated
questions.explanation: DIC paradoxically causes hemorrhage because hemostatic elements are depleted during widespread clotting.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.topic: Fate and Clinical Consequences of Thrombi, including DIC
questions.prompt: Embolization means a thrombus:
options: Detaches and travels to another vascular site
questions.answer: Detaches and travels to another vascular site
questions.explanation: Fragments of thrombi can travel and lodge downstream as emboli.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.topic: Fate and Clinical Consequences of Thrombi, including DIC
questions.prompt: Thrombus dissolution is most likely when:
options: Fibrinolysis occurs early in a recent thrombus
A thrombus is old and densely organized
questions.answer: Fibrinolysis occurs early in a recent thrombus
questions.explanation: Recent thrombi may be removed by fibrinolytic activity.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.topic: Fate and Clinical Consequences of Thrombi, including DIC
questions.prompt: Organization of a thrombus involves:
options: Ingrowth of endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, and fibroblasts
questions.answer: Ingrowth of endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, and fibroblasts
questions.explanation: Older thrombi may be incorporated into the vessel wall by repair tissue.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.topic: Fate and Clinical Consequences of Thrombi, including DIC
questions.prompt: Recanalization refers to:
options: Complete obstruction by a fresh embolus
Formation of channels through an organized thrombus
questions.answer: Formation of channels through an organized thrombus
questions.explanation: Channels may restore limited blood flow across an organized thrombus.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.topic: Fate and Clinical Consequences of Thrombi, including DIC
questions.prompt: The most important clinical consequence of venous thrombosis is often:
questions.explanation: Deep venous thrombi can embolize through the right heart to pulmonary arteries.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.topic: Fate and Clinical Consequences of Thrombi, including DIC
questions.prompt: The most important clinical consequence of arterial thrombosis is often:
questions.explanation: Arterial thrombi can occlude blood supply to organs such as heart, brain, or bowel.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.topic: Fate and Clinical Consequences of Thrombi, including DIC
questions.prompt: Disseminated intravascular coagulation is best described as:
options: Widespread microvascular thrombosis with consumption of platelets and coagulation factors
questions.answer: Widespread microvascular thrombosis with consumption of platelets and coagulation factors
questions.explanation: DIC consumes clotting components while forming microthrombi, causing both thrombosis and bleeding.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.topic: Fate and Clinical Consequences of Thrombi, including DIC
questions.prompt: A classic trigger of DIC is:
options: Obstetric complications, sepsis, or advanced malignancy
questions.answer: Obstetric complications, sepsis, or advanced malignancy
questions.explanation: DIC is secondary to disorders that strongly activate coagulation systemically.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: The first immediate response to vascular injury is usually:
questions.explanation: Neurogenic reflexes and endothelin cause brief vasoconstriction that reduces blood loss.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Thrombin is central to hemostasis because it:
options: Converts fibrinogen to fibrin and activates platelets
questions.answer: Converts fibrinogen to fibrin and activates platelets
questions.explanation: Thrombin amplifies coagulation, activates platelets, and generates fibrin.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Primary hemostasis produces:
questions.explanation: Primary hemostasis depends on platelet adhesion, activation, and aggregation.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Secondary hemostasis stabilizes the platelet plug mainly by forming:
questions.explanation: The coagulation cascade generates thrombin, which converts fibrinogen to fibrin.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Platelet adhesion to subendothelial matrix is mediated largely by:
questions.explanation: vWF bridges exposed matrix and platelet GpIb, allowing adhesion under flow.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Platelet aggregation is mediated mainly by:
options: GpIIb/IIIa binding fibrinogen bridges between platelets
questions.answer: GpIIb/IIIa binding fibrinogen bridges between platelets
questions.explanation: Activated GpIIb/IIIa binds fibrinogen, linking adjacent platelets.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Dense granules of platelets contain important mediators such as:
questions.explanation: Dense granules release ADP and calcium, which support platelet activation and coagulation.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Aspirin impairs platelet function by inhibiting synthesis of:
questions.explanation: Aspirin blocks platelet cyclooxygenase, reducing TxA2-mediated aggregation.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Bernard-Soulier syndrome causes bleeding because of defective:
questions.explanation: GpIb deficiency impairs platelet adhesion to vWF.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is caused by deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Loss of GpIIb/IIIa prevents fibrinogen-mediated platelet aggregation.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: An infarct is:
questions.explanation: Infarction is tissue necrosis caused by loss of blood supply or venous drainage.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Microscopic evidence of necrosis after vascular occlusion may be absent for the first:
questions.explanation: Histologic necrosis typically requires hours to become apparent after ischemic injury.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Most infarcts are caused by:
questions.explanation: Arterial occlusion by thrombi or emboli is the most common cause.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: White infarcts usually occur in:
options: Loose spongy tissues with dual blood supply
questions.explanation: Pale infarcts occur in compact tissues where arterial inflow is blocked and little blood can enter.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Red infarcts are likely with:
options: End-arterial occlusion in compact kidney only
Venous occlusion or tissues with dual blood supply
questions.answer: Venous occlusion or tissues with dual blood supply
questions.explanation: Hemorrhagic infarcts occur when blood can enter necrotic tissue or when venous drainage is blocked.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Pulmonary infarcts are often red because the lung:
options: Has dual blood supply and spongy parenchyma
questions.answer: Has dual blood supply and spongy parenchyma
questions.explanation: Bronchial and pulmonary arterial supplies and loose tissue architecture favor hemorrhagic infarction.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: The dominant histologic pattern in most non-brain infarcts is:
questions.explanation: Ischemia usually produces coagulative necrosis except in the brain.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Brain infarction characteristically produces:
options: Coagulative necrosis with firm scar at once
questions.explanation: CNS ischemic injury causes liquefactive necrosis.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Whether vascular occlusion causes infarction depends strongly on:
options: Collateral supply, rate of occlusion, tissue susceptibility, and oxygen content
questions.answer: Collateral supply, rate of occlusion, tissue susceptibility, and oxygen content
questions.explanation: Robbins emphasizes these determinants of infarct development.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: A septic infarct means:
options: The infarct is infected or seeded by microbes
The infarct is always pale and sterile
The infarct is caused only by albumin loss
The infarct is a postmortem clot
questions.answer: The infarct is infected or seeded by microbes
questions.explanation: Septic emboli can seed organisms into infarcted tissue and form abscesses.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Shock is best defined as:
options: Systemic tissue hypoperfusion from reduced cardiac output or effective circulating volume
A platelet plug at an injury site
questions.answer: Systemic tissue hypoperfusion from reduced cardiac output or effective circulating volume
questions.explanation: Shock is circulatory failure that causes cellular hypoxia and organ dysfunction.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Septic shock commonly causes microvascular thrombosis because inflammatory cytokines:
options: Increase tissue factor, reduce anticoagulants, and increase PAI-1
questions.answer: Increase tissue factor, reduce anticoagulants, and increase PAI-1
questions.explanation: Sepsis promotes coagulation and inhibits fibrinolysis, leading to DIC and tissue ischemia.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: The three major types of shock are:
questions.explanation: Robbins emphasizes cardiogenic, hypovolemic, and septic shock as major categories.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Cardiogenic shock can be caused by:
questions.explanation: Pump failure after MI can reduce cardiac output and perfusion.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Hypovolemic shock can result from:
questions.explanation: Loss of blood or plasma volume reduces effective circulating volume.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Early septic shock may show warm, flushed skin because of:
questions.explanation: Unlike hypovolemic/cardiogenic shock, early sepsis often causes vasodilation.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: A key feature of septic shock pathogenesis is:
options: Only loss of albumin in urine
Dysregulated host response with endothelial activation, vasodilation, leakage, and DIC
questions.answer: Dysregulated host response with endothelial activation, vasodilation, leakage, and DIC
questions.explanation: Septic shock is driven by inflammatory mediators, endothelial dysfunction, coagulation activation, and metabolic abnormalities.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: The initial nonprogressive stage of shock maintains perfusion through:
questions.explanation: Baroreflexes, catecholamines, ADH, and RAAS help preserve blood pressure and vital organ flow.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: The progressive stage of shock is characterized by:
options: Tissue hypoperfusion with lactic acidosis and worsening circulatory failure
questions.answer: Tissue hypoperfusion with lactic acidosis and worsening circulatory failure
questions.explanation: Persistent hypoxia shifts metabolism to anaerobic glycolysis, causing lactic acidosis and vasomotor failure.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Irreversible shock means:
options: The patient has only mild hypotension
Cellular injury is so severe that survival is impossible even if hemodynamics are corrected
questions.answer: Cellular injury is so severe that survival is impossible even if hemodynamics are corrected
questions.explanation: Late shock produces severe cellular and organ injury that cannot be reversed by restoring pressure alone.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Virchow triad consists of endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow, and:
questions.explanation: These three factors are the major contributors to pathologic thrombosis.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Mural thrombi are thrombi that:
options: Form on the wall of a heart chamber or large vessel
questions.answer: Form on the wall of a heart chamber or large vessel
questions.explanation: Mural thrombi are attached to endocardial or vascular walls, often after MI or in aneurysms.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Arterial thrombi are typically rich in:
questions.explanation: High-shear arterial thrombi depend strongly on platelet adhesion and activation.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Venous thrombi are typically:
options: Red cell-rich and associated with stasis
questions.answer: Red cell-rich and associated with stasis
questions.explanation: Slow venous flow promotes coagulation and traps red cells, forming red thrombi.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Lines of Zahn indicate:
options: Antemortem thrombus formation in flowing blood
questions.answer: Antemortem thrombus formation in flowing blood
questions.explanation: Alternating pale platelet/fibrin and dark red cell layers form only when blood is flowing.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Endothelial injury promotes thrombosis by:
questions.explanation: Injury exposes prothrombotic matrix and tissue factor, triggering platelets and coagulation.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Stasis promotes thrombosis partly because it:
options: Prevents dilution and washout of activated clotting factors
questions.answer: Prevents dilution and washout of activated clotting factors
questions.explanation: Stasis keeps activated factors near the vessel wall and brings platelets into contact with endothelium.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Turbulence promotes arterial thrombosis by:
options: Causing endothelial dysfunction and local pockets of stasis
questions.answer: Causing endothelial dysfunction and local pockets of stasis
questions.explanation: Disturbed flow injures/activates endothelium and disrupts laminar flow.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Factor V Leiden causes hypercoagulability because factor V becomes resistant to:
questions.explanation: The Leiden mutation impairs APC-mediated inactivation of factor Va.

questions.chapterTitle: Hemodynamic Disorders, Thromboembolic Disease, and Shock
questions.prompt: Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome is paradoxically associated clinically with:
options: Thrombosis despite prolonged phospholipid-dependent clotting tests in vitro
questions.answer: Thrombosis despite prolonged phospholipid-dependent clotting tests in vitro
questions.explanation: Antiphospholipid antibodies may prolong PTT assays yet cause arterial/venous thrombosis and pregnancy morbidity.

questions.prompt: Down syndrome is most commonly caused by:
questions.explanation: Most cases of Down syndrome result from an extra chromosome 21 due to nondisjunction.

questions.prompt: Mosaic Down syndrome is usually milder because:
options: Only a proportion of cells carry trisomy 21
All cells carry four copies of chromosome 21
It is caused by LDL receptor mutation
questions.answer: Only a proportion of cells carry trisomy 21
questions.explanation: Phenotype depends partly on the fraction and distribution of trisomic cells.

questions.prompt: A major risk factor for trisomy 21 is:
questions.explanation: Maternal age strongly increases risk of meiotic nondisjunction.

questions.prompt: Children with Down syndrome have increased risk of:
questions.explanation: Down syndrome is associated with increased risk of ALL and AML, especially megakaryoblastic leukemia.

questions.prompt: A congenital heart defect classically associated with Down syndrome is:
questions.explanation: Endocardial cushion defects, including AV septal defects, are common in Down syndrome.

questions.prompt: A Robertsonian translocation involving chromosome 21 can cause:
questions.explanation: A parent carrying a balanced Robertsonian translocation can have children with extra 21q material.

questions.prompt: Edwards syndrome is:
questions.explanation: Trisomy 18 is Edwards syndrome.

questions.prompt: Patau syndrome is:
questions.explanation: Trisomy 13 is Patau syndrome.

questions.prompt: Chromosome 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is strongly associated with abnormal development of:
questions.explanation: 22q11.2 deletion affects pharyngeal pouch development, causing thymic/parathyroid and cardiac defects.

questions.prompt: A child with thymic hypoplasia, hypocalcemia, and conotruncal cardiac defects most likely has:
questions.explanation: DiGeorge/22q11.2 deletion syndrome causes T-cell deficiency, hypocalcemia, and conotruncal anomalies.

questions.topic: Complex Multigenic Disorders and Cytogenetic Principles
questions.prompt: Complex multigenic disorders result from:
options: A single mutation with classic Mendelian inheritance only
Interactions of multiple genes and environmental factors
questions.answer: Interactions of multiple genes and environmental factors
questions.explanation: Common diseases often reflect multiple susceptibility genes plus environmental influences.

questions.topic: Complex Multigenic Disorders and Cytogenetic Principles
questions.prompt: Genetic linkage analysis uses polymorphic markers because:
options: They replace karyotyping for all aneuploidies
Marker alleles can track inheritance of nearby disease loci in families
questions.answer: Marker alleles can track inheritance of nearby disease loci in families
questions.explanation: Markers such as microsatellites can identify inheritance patterns near a disease gene.

questions.topic: Complex Multigenic Disorders and Cytogenetic Principles
questions.prompt: A normal human somatic karyotype contains:
questions.explanation: Human somatic cells normally have 22 pairs of autosomes and two sex chromosomes.

questions.topic: Complex Multigenic Disorders and Cytogenetic Principles
questions.prompt: Aneuploidy means:
options: Chromosome number is not an exact multiple of the haploid number
A point mutation in one codon
questions.answer: Chromosome number is not an exact multiple of the haploid number
questions.explanation: Monosomy and trisomy are forms of aneuploidy.

questions.topic: Complex Multigenic Disorders and Cytogenetic Principles
questions.prompt: Nondisjunction is:
options: Exchange of equal chromosomal segments only
Failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate
questions.answer: Failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate
questions.explanation: Nondisjunction during meiosis is a major cause of aneuploidy.

questions.topic: Complex Multigenic Disorders and Cytogenetic Principles
questions.prompt: Mosaicism means:
options: Every cell has the same mutation inherited from both parents
Two or more genetically distinct cell lines in one individual
questions.answer: Two or more genetically distinct cell lines in one individual
questions.explanation: Postzygotic errors can create genetically different cell populations.

questions.topic: Complex Multigenic Disorders and Cytogenetic Principles
questions.prompt: A balanced reciprocal translocation is often clinically silent because:
options: No essential genetic material is gained or lost
questions.answer: No essential genetic material is gained or lost
questions.explanation: Balanced rearrangements may preserve gene dosage, although they can disrupt genes or affect offspring.

questions.topic: Complex Multigenic Disorders and Cytogenetic Principles
questions.prompt: A Robertsonian translocation involves fusion of:
options: Long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes
Two sister chromatids at every centromere
questions.answer: Long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes
questions.explanation: Robertsonian translocations join acrocentric long arms and can underlie familial Down syndrome.

questions.topic: Complex Multigenic Disorders and Cytogenetic Principles
questions.prompt: A ring chromosome forms after:
options: Breaks at both chromosome ends with fusion of the broken ends
questions.answer: Breaks at both chromosome ends with fusion of the broken ends
questions.explanation: Loss of terminal segments and end-to-end fusion creates a ring chromosome.

questions.topic: Complex Multigenic Disorders and Cytogenetic Principles
questions.prompt: An inversion is pericentric when it:
questions.explanation: Pericentric inversions involve breaks on both sides of the centromere.

questions.prompt: Lysosomal storage diseases usually result from:
options: Inherited deficiency of a lysosomal enzyme or related protein
questions.answer: Inherited deficiency of a lysosomal enzyme or related protein
questions.explanation: Failure of lysosomal degradation causes accumulation of undegraded substrates.

questions.prompt: Lysosomal storage disorders often show organomegaly because:
options: Storage material accumulates in mononuclear phagocytes and parenchymal cells
questions.answer: Storage material accumulates in mononuclear phagocytes and parenchymal cells
questions.explanation: Progressive substrate accumulation expands affected cells and organs.

questions.prompt: Tay-Sachs disease is caused by deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Tay-Sachs disease results from HEXA mutations and GM2 ganglioside accumulation.

questions.prompt: Gaucher disease is caused by deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Gaucher disease is a lysosomal storage disorder involving glucocerebroside accumulation.

questions.prompt: A cherry-red spot may be seen in:
questions.explanation: Ganglioside accumulation in retinal ganglion cells can leave the fovea appearing cherry red.

questions.prompt: Gaucher cells have a characteristic cytoplasm described as:
questions.explanation: Lipid-laden macrophages in Gaucher disease have fibrillary, wrinkled cytoplasm.

questions.prompt: Niemann-Pick disease types A and B involve deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Types A and B Niemann-Pick disease are caused by sphingomyelinase deficiency.

questions.prompt: Niemann-Pick disease type C is primarily a defect in:
questions.explanation: NPC1/NPC2 defects impair cholesterol movement out of lysosomes.

questions.prompt: I-cell disease occurs because lysosomal enzymes:
options: Fail to receive mannose-6-phosphate targeting markers
Are encoded only by the Y chromosome
questions.answer: Fail to receive mannose-6-phosphate targeting markers
questions.explanation: Without mannose-6-phosphate, lysosomal enzymes are secreted rather than delivered to lysosomes.

questions.prompt: Pompe disease is a glycogen storage disease caused by deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Pompe disease is glycogen storage disease type II and affects lysosomal glycogen degradation.

questions.topic: Receptor and Transport Protein Disorders: Familial Hypercholesterolemia
questions.prompt: Familial hypercholesterolemia most commonly involves defective:
questions.explanation: Reduced LDL receptor function decreases hepatic LDL uptake.

questions.topic: Receptor and Transport Protein Disorders: Familial Hypercholesterolemia
questions.prompt: Statins are useful in many patients with familial hypercholesterolemia because they:
options: Repair the LDL receptor gene directly
Increase hepatic LDL receptor expression by lowering intracellular cholesterol synthesis
Block all cholesterol absorption in lysosomes
questions.answer: Increase hepatic LDL receptor expression by lowering intracellular cholesterol synthesis
questions.explanation: By inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase, statins increase LDL receptor expression when receptor function remains.

questions.topic: Receptor and Transport Protein Disorders: Familial Hypercholesterolemia
questions.prompt: The major plasma lipid abnormality in familial hypercholesterolemia is:
questions.explanation: LDL accumulates in plasma when receptor-mediated clearance is impaired.

questions.topic: Receptor and Transport Protein Disorders: Familial Hypercholesterolemia
questions.prompt: A clinical finding associated with familial hypercholesterolemia is:
questions.explanation: Cholesterol-rich deposits in tendons and skin can form xanthomas.

questions.topic: Receptor and Transport Protein Disorders: Familial Hypercholesterolemia
questions.prompt: The most serious consequence of familial hypercholesterolemia is:
options: Premature atherosclerosis and coronary artery disease
questions.answer: Premature atherosclerosis and coronary artery disease
questions.explanation: High LDL accelerates atheroma formation and vascular disease.

questions.topic: Receptor and Transport Protein Disorders: Familial Hypercholesterolemia
questions.prompt: LDL receptors are normally clustered in membrane regions called:
questions.explanation: LDL binds receptors in coated pits, which are internalized by endocytosis.

questions.topic: Receptor and Transport Protein Disorders: Familial Hypercholesterolemia
questions.prompt: After LDL receptor-mediated endocytosis, LDL is degraded mainly in:
questions.explanation: The LDL particle dissociates from its receptor and is degraded in lysosomes.

questions.topic: Receptor and Transport Protein Disorders: Familial Hypercholesterolemia
questions.prompt: PCSK9 promotes hypercholesterolemia by:
questions.explanation: PCSK9 binds LDL receptors and targets them for degradation after endocytosis.

questions.topic: Receptor and Transport Protein Disorders: Familial Hypercholesterolemia
questions.prompt: A homozygous LDL receptor defect is more severe than heterozygous disease because:
options: LDL is cleared by red cells only
LDL receptor activity is nearly absent rather than partially reduced
questions.answer: LDL receptor activity is nearly absent rather than partially reduced
questions.explanation: Gene dosage strongly affects LDL clearance and age of cardiovascular disease onset.

questions.topic: Receptor and Transport Protein Disorders: Familial Hypercholesterolemia
questions.prompt: Intracellular cholesterol normally suppresses cholesterol synthesis by inhibiting:
questions.explanation: Free cholesterol downregulates HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol synthesis.

questions.prompt: A missense mutation is best defined as:
options: A base substitution that changes one amino acid to another
A mutation that creates a premature stop codon
A deletion of an entire chromosome
A repeat expansion that always silences a gene
questions.answer: A base substitution that changes one amino acid to another
questions.explanation: Missense mutations alter the meaning of a codon and substitute one amino acid in the protein.

questions.prompt: Genetic heterogeneity means:
options: One mutation always produces many unrelated effects
Mutations at different loci can produce a similar clinical phenotype
A gene is expressed only from the paternal allele
questions.answer: Mutations at different loci can produce a similar clinical phenotype
questions.explanation: Clinically similar disorders such as childhood deafness may arise from mutations in many different genes.

questions.prompt: A nonsense mutation produces disease by:
options: Replacing one amino acid with a similar amino acid
Changing an amino acid codon into a stop codon
questions.answer: Changing an amino acid codon into a stop codon
questions.explanation: Nonsense mutations create premature termination codons, often yielding truncated unstable proteins.

questions.prompt: A frameshift mutation usually results from:
options: Insertion or deletion of bases not in multiples of three
questions.answer: Insertion or deletion of bases not in multiples of three
questions.explanation: Because codons are read in triplets, non-triplet insertions or deletions alter the downstream reading frame.

questions.prompt: A mutation in a promoter or enhancer may cause disease mainly by:
options: Changing the number of chromosomes in every cell
questions.explanation: Regulatory sequence mutations can impair transcription factor binding and reduce mRNA production.

questions.prompt: A point mutation in an intron can be pathogenic when it:
questions.explanation: Intronic splice-site mutations can prevent proper processing of the primary RNA transcript.

questions.prompt: A conservative missense mutation is usually less harmful because:
options: The substituted amino acid has similar biochemical properties
It always restores the normal codon
It creates a full chromosomal monosomy
questions.answer: The substituted amino acid has similar biochemical properties
questions.explanation: A chemically similar substitution may preserve enough protein structure and function.

questions.prompt: The sickle cell mutation is a classic example of:
questions.explanation: Sickle hemoglobin results from substitution of valine for glutamic acid in beta-globin, changing protein properties.

questions.prompt: A three-base-pair deletion within a coding exon is less likely to cause a frameshift because:
options: All deletions are corrected by mismatch repair
The reading frame remains aligned after loss of one codon
questions.answer: The reading frame remains aligned after loss of one codon
questions.explanation: In-frame deletions remove amino acid(s) but preserve codon grouping downstream.

questions.prompt: Pleiotropism means:
options: One mutant gene produces multiple phenotypic effects
Several genes produce the same phenotype
questions.answer: One mutant gene produces multiple phenotypic effects
questions.explanation: Sickle cell disease is pleiotropic because one beta-globin mutation causes anemia, vaso-occlusion, organ infarcts, and more.

questions.prompt: Autosomal dominant disorders are typically expressed in:
questions.explanation: A single mutant autosomal allele is sufficient to produce many dominant phenotypes.

questions.prompt: A new mutation is especially common in severe autosomal dominant disorders because:
options: Autosomal genes mutate only after birth
Affected individuals often have reduced reproductive fitness
questions.answer: Affected individuals often have reduced reproductive fitness
questions.explanation: When disease limits reproduction, many cases arise from new germline mutations rather than inheritance.

questions.prompt: If an affected heterozygous parent has an autosomal dominant disorder and the other parent is unaffected, each child has what risk?
questions.explanation: Each child has a one-in-two chance of inheriting the mutant allele.

questions.prompt: Autosomal recessive disorders usually require:
options: A mutant allele only on the Y chromosome
One dominant allele in every affected person
Mutant alleles on both homologous chromosomes
questions.answer: Mutant alleles on both homologous chromosomes
questions.explanation: Most autosomal recessive diseases manifest in homozygotes or compound heterozygotes.

questions.prompt: A key reason autosomal recessive disorders are more common in consanguineous families is:
options: Relatives are more likely to carry the same rare mutant allele
questions.answer: Relatives are more likely to carry the same rare mutant allele
questions.explanation: Shared ancestry increases the chance both parents carry the same pathogenic recessive variant.

questions.prompt: Incomplete penetrance means:
options: The phenotype is always identical in all carriers
Some individuals with the disease genotype do not express the phenotype
The gene is located only in mitochondria
questions.answer: Some individuals with the disease genotype do not express the phenotype
questions.explanation: Penetrance describes the proportion of genotype-positive individuals who show the trait.

questions.prompt: Variable expressivity means:
options: Only half of carriers have any phenotype
All daughters of affected fathers are unaffected
