questions.explanation: ANA and anti-dsDNA/anti-Sm antibodies are characteristic of SLE.

questions.prompt: A patient develops tight skin of the fingers, Raynaud phenomenon, dysphagia from esophageal fibrosis, and pulmonary hypertension. The disease involves endothelial injury and fibroblast activation rather than immune complex deposition alone. Which disease fits best?
questions.explanation: Systemic sclerosis is marked by vasculopathy and progressive fibrosis of skin and organs.

questions.prompt: The most specific antibody for SLE among common tests is:
questions.explanation: Anti-Sm is highly specific, though not very sensitive, for SLE.

questions.prompt: Sjögren syndrome primarily affects:
questions.explanation: Autoimmune destruction of exocrine glands causes dry eyes and dry mouth.

questions.prompt: Anti-dsDNA antibodies in SLE correlate especially with:
questions.explanation: Anti-dsDNA immune complexes are associated with renal involvement.

questions.prompt: Libman-Sacks endocarditis in SLE is characterized by:
options: Sterile vegetations on either side of valve leaflets
questions.answer: Sterile vegetations on either side of valve leaflets
questions.explanation: SLE can cause sterile verrucous endocarditis.

questions.prompt: Sjögren syndrome increases risk of:
questions.explanation: Chronic B-cell stimulation in Sjögren syndrome predisposes to MALT-type lymphoma.

questions.prompt: Systemic sclerosis is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Scleroderma combines vascular injury, immune activation, and collagen deposition.

questions.prompt: A woman has photosensitive malar rash, arthritis, low complement, and proteinuria. Renal biopsy shows granular deposits of IgG and complement in glomeruli. Which mechanism best explains the nephritis?
options: Type III immune complex disease due to anti-nuclear antibodies
questions.answer: Type III immune complex disease due to anti-nuclear antibodies
questions.explanation: SLE nephritis is largely immune complex-mediated, producing granular deposits.

questions.prompt: A patient has dry eyes, dry mouth, parotid enlargement, anti-SSA antibodies, and a monoclonal B-cell proliferation in salivary tissue. Which long-term complication is most directly linked to the chronic autoimmune process?
questions.explanation: Sjögren syndrome may evolve into extranodal marginal zone lymphoma from chronic B-cell activation.

questions.prompt: The major barrier to organ transplantation is mismatch in:
questions.explanation: HLA polymorphism is the main determinant of graft recognition.

questions.prompt: After bone marrow transplantation, a recipient develops rash, jaundice, diarrhea, and mucosal ulceration. The graft contains mature donor T cells, and the recipient is immunosuppressed. Which immunologic event is central?
options: Recipient IgE against donor mast cells
Preformed recipient antibodies to kidney endothelium
Donor T cells reacting against recipient antigens
questions.answer: Donor T cells reacting against recipient antigens
questions.explanation: GVHD occurs when donor T cells recognize host alloantigens.

questions.prompt: Hyperacute rejection is usually mediated by:
questions.explanation: Preexisting antibodies cause immediate endothelial injury and thrombosis.

questions.prompt: Graft-versus-host disease occurs when:
options: Donor T cells attack recipient tissues
Recipient antibodies attack donor RBCs only
questions.answer: Donor T cells attack recipient tissues
questions.explanation: Immunocompetent donor T cells react against host antigens.

questions.prompt: Acute cellular rejection is mediated mainly by:
questions.explanation: Recipient T cells attack graft parenchyma and vessels.

questions.prompt: Acute antibody-mediated rejection primarily targets:
questions.explanation: Antibodies to donor antigens injure graft vessels through complement and inflammation.

questions.prompt: Chronic rejection is characterized by:
options: Progressive vascular narrowing and interstitial fibrosis
questions.answer: Progressive vascular narrowing and interstitial fibrosis
questions.explanation: Chronic rejection causes graft ischemia and fibrosis over months to years.

questions.prompt: Direct allorecognition means recipient T cells recognize:
options: Intact donor MHC molecules on donor APCs
Only donor peptides on recipient MHC
questions.answer: Intact donor MHC molecules on donor APCs
questions.explanation: Direct recognition is a strong T-cell response to foreign MHC itself.

questions.prompt: Minutes after kidney transplantation, the graft becomes cyanotic and fails to perfuse. Histology shows neutrophils, fibrin thrombi, and endothelial injury. The recipient had circulating antibodies against donor blood group/HLA antigens. What is the rejection pattern?
questions.explanation: Preformed antibodies cause immediate complement-mediated vascular thrombosis.

questions.prompt: Months after transplant, a patient develops gradual renal graft dysfunction. Biopsy shows intimal smooth muscle proliferation, luminal narrowing, tubular atrophy, and interstitial fibrosis. There is no sudden thrombosed graft. Which process is most likely?
questions.explanation: Chronic rejection is dominated by vascular occlusion and fibrosis.

questions.topic: Characteristics of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms
questions.prompt: The most reliable feature proving malignancy in a solid tumor is:
questions.explanation: Metastasis is unequivocal evidence of malignancy in solid tumors.

questions.topic: Characteristics of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms
questions.prompt: A large uterine smooth muscle tumor has infiltrative edges, hemorrhage, necrosis, numerous atypical mitoses, and pleomorphic cells. A small well-circumscribed smooth muscle mass elsewhere in the uterus lacks these findings. Which feature most supports leiomyosarcoma?
options: Invasion with cytologic atypia and abnormal mitotic activity
questions.answer: Invasion with cytologic atypia and abnormal mitotic activity
questions.explanation: Malignant smooth muscle tumors show infiltrative growth, atypia, necrosis, and mitoses.

questions.topic: Characteristics of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms
questions.prompt: Differentiation refers to:
options: Resemblance of tumor cells to normal cells of origin
questions.answer: Resemblance of tumor cells to normal cells of origin
questions.explanation: Differentiation measures morphologic and functional similarity to normal tissue.

questions.topic: Characteristics of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms
questions.prompt: Anaplasia means:
questions.explanation: Anaplasia is a hallmark of many malignant tumors.

questions.topic: Characteristics of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms
questions.prompt: Carcinoma in situ means malignant epithelial cells:
options: Involve full epithelial thickness without basement membrane invasion
questions.answer: Involve full epithelial thickness without basement membrane invasion
questions.explanation: In situ carcinoma shows cytologic malignancy but remains above the basement membrane.

questions.topic: Characteristics of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms
questions.prompt: Dysplasia is most often recognized by:
options: Orderly maturation with tiny uniform nuclei
Disordered epithelial growth with pleomorphism and architectural loss
questions.answer: Disordered epithelial growth with pleomorphism and architectural loss
questions.explanation: Dysplasia is premalignant epithelial disordered growth.

questions.topic: Characteristics of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms
questions.prompt: Benign tumors usually grow by:
options: Diffuse infiltration of all adjacent structures
questions.explanation: Benign tumors often push aside adjacent tissue rather than invade it.

questions.topic: Characteristics of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms
questions.prompt: Which feature favors malignancy over benignity?
options: Tumor giant cells with abnormal mitoses
questions.answer: Tumor giant cells with abnormal mitoses
questions.explanation: Marked pleomorphism and atypical mitoses suggest anaplasia and malignancy.

questions.topic: Characteristics of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms
questions.prompt: A cervical biopsy shows full-thickness epithelial atypia, loss of maturation, hyperchromatic nuclei, and mitoses above the basal layer. The basement membrane is intact, and no stromal invasion is identified. Which diagnosis best matches these findings?
questions.explanation: Full-thickness dysplasia without basement membrane invasion is carcinoma in situ.

questions.topic: Characteristics of Benign and Malignant Neoplasms
questions.prompt: A smoker’s bronchial biopsy shows replacement of ciliated columnar epithelium by squamous epithelium. A later biopsy shows pleomorphic basal-like cells and abnormal mitoses, but no invasion. Which sequence best describes the progression?
options: Metaplasia to dysplasia to carcinoma in situ
questions.answer: Metaplasia to dysplasia to carcinoma in situ
questions.explanation: Chronic injury can cause metaplasia, then dysplasia, then preinvasive carcinoma.

questions.topic: Clinical Features, Grading, Staging, and Laboratory Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Tumor grade is based mainly on:
options: Degree of differentiation and mitotic activity
questions.answer: Degree of differentiation and mitotic activity
questions.explanation: Grade estimates biologic aggressiveness from histology.

questions.topic: Clinical Features, Grading, Staging, and Laboratory Diagnosis
questions.prompt: A man with pancreatic carcinoma loses marked weight despite adequate caloric intake and no mechanical obstruction. He has muscle wasting, anorexia, and elevated inflammatory mediators. Which mechanism best explains this systemic effect?
options: Cancer cachexia mediated by cytokines and metabolic changes
questions.answer: Cancer cachexia mediated by cytokines and metabolic changes
questions.explanation: Cachexia is a cytokine-driven wasting syndrome not fully reversed by nutrition.

questions.topic: Clinical Features, Grading, Staging, and Laboratory Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Tumor stage is based mainly on:
options: Size/local extent, nodal spread, and distant metastasis
questions.answer: Size/local extent, nodal spread, and distant metastasis
questions.explanation: Stage describes anatomic spread, often by TNM.

questions.topic: Clinical Features, Grading, Staging, and Laboratory Diagnosis
questions.prompt: For most solid tumors, prognosis correlates better with:
questions.explanation: Anatomic extent is usually more prognostically important than grade.

questions.topic: Clinical Features, Grading, Staging, and Laboratory Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Cachexia in cancer is driven partly by:
questions.explanation: Cancer cachexia involves systemic inflammation and metabolic wasting.

questions.topic: Clinical Features, Grading, Staging, and Laboratory Diagnosis
questions.prompt: Paraneoplastic syndromes are symptoms caused by:
options: Only direct compression by tumor mass
Hormone-like or immune effects not explained by local tumor spread
questions.answer: Hormone-like or immune effects not explained by local tumor spread
questions.explanation: Paraneoplastic syndromes are remote effects of cancer.

questions.topic: Clinical Features, Grading, Staging, and Laboratory Diagnosis
questions.prompt: A classic paraneoplastic endocrine syndrome in small cell lung carcinoma is:
questions.explanation: Small cell carcinoma may secrete ACTH or ADH.

questions.topic: Clinical Features, Grading, Staging, and Laboratory Diagnosis
questions.prompt: A definitive cancer diagnosis most often requires:
questions.explanation: Tissue diagnosis remains central to tumor classification.

questions.topic: Clinical Features, Grading, Staging, and Laboratory Diagnosis
questions.prompt: A colon cancer invades through muscularis propria and has metastases in regional lymph nodes but no distant metastasis. Another colon cancer is poorly differentiated but confined to mucosa. Which parameter usually has greater prognostic weight?
options: Presence of a capsule in all cancers
questions.explanation: Stage generally predicts outcome better than grade in most solid tumors.

questions.topic: Clinical Features, Grading, Staging, and Laboratory Diagnosis
questions.prompt: A patient with lung cancer develops hypercalcemia, but imaging shows no bone metastases. Laboratory testing reveals tumor production of a parathyroid hormone-related peptide. Which clinical category best explains this finding?
questions.explanation: PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia is a paraneoplastic endocrine syndrome.

questions.topic: DNA Repair Defects and Genomic Instability
questions.prompt: Defective DNA repair predisposes to cancer by causing:
questions.explanation: Failure to repair DNA damage increases mutation rates.

questions.topic: DNA Repair Defects and Genomic Instability
questions.prompt: A woman with inherited BRCA1 mutation develops high-grade serous carcinoma. The tumor is defective in homologous recombination repair, making it vulnerable to PARP inhibition through synthetic lethality. Which lesion is normally repaired by BRCA pathways?
questions.explanation: BRCA1/2 are essential for homologous recombination repair of double-strand DNA breaks.

questions.topic: DNA Repair Defects and Genomic Instability
questions.prompt: Mismatch repair defects are associated with:
questions.explanation: Mismatch repair loss causes length changes in microsatellite repeats.

questions.topic: DNA Repair Defects and Genomic Instability
questions.prompt: BRCA1 and BRCA2 participate in repair of:
options: Double-strand DNA breaks by homologous recombination
questions.answer: Double-strand DNA breaks by homologous recombination
questions.explanation: BRCA proteins help high-fidelity double-strand break repair.

questions.topic: DNA Repair Defects and Genomic Instability
questions.prompt: Lynch syndrome is caused by germline defects in:
questions.explanation: Inherited mismatch repair defects predispose to colon and endometrial cancers.

questions.topic: DNA Repair Defects and Genomic Instability
questions.prompt: Xeroderma pigmentosum results from defective:
questions.explanation: XP impairs repair of UV-induced pyrimidine dimers.

questions.topic: DNA Repair Defects and Genomic Instability
questions.prompt: Microsatellite instability is most useful as a marker of:
questions.explanation: MSI reflects insertion/deletion errors at short repeats due to MMR loss.

questions.topic: DNA Repair Defects and Genomic Instability
questions.prompt: Cancers with high mutation burdens may be more responsive to immune checkpoint blockade because they:
questions.explanation: More mutations can create tumor-specific peptides recognized by T cells.

questions.topic: DNA Repair Defects and Genomic Instability
questions.prompt: A young patient develops colon cancer, and tumor testing shows loss of MLH1/MSH2 function with length variation in multiple microsatellite markers. The tumor has numerous frameshift mutations in growth-regulatory genes. Which inherited syndrome is most likely?
questions.explanation: Lynch syndrome is caused by germline mismatch repair defects and MSI.

questions.topic: DNA Repair Defects and Genomic Instability
questions.prompt: A child develops multiple skin cancers on sun-exposed areas, severe photosensitivity, and inability to repair UV-induced pyrimidine dimers. The underlying defect lies in excising bulky helix-distorting lesions. Which repair pathway is abnormal?
questions.explanation: Xeroderma pigmentosum involves nucleotide excision repair defects.

questions.topic: Molecular Basis and Hallmarks of Cancer
questions.prompt: Cancer is fundamentally caused by:
options: Genetic and epigenetic alterations in a cell clone
questions.answer: Genetic and epigenetic alterations in a cell clone
questions.explanation: Neoplasms arise from heritable changes that confer growth and survival advantages.

questions.topic: Molecular Basis and Hallmarks of Cancer
questions.prompt: A small carcinoma remains clinically dormant until a clone emerges that secretes VEGF, degrades basement membrane, and survives in blood. The new clone expands because it has a selective advantage within the tumor. What process best explains this evolution?
questions.explanation: Tumors evolve by selection of subclones with advantageous mutations.

questions.topic: Molecular Basis and Hallmarks of Cancer
questions.prompt: Driver mutations are mutations that:
questions.explanation: Drivers provide selective growth, survival, or invasion advantages.

questions.topic: Molecular Basis and Hallmarks of Cancer
questions.prompt: Passenger mutations are:
options: Incidental mutations not directly contributing to tumor behavior
questions.answer: Incidental mutations not directly contributing to tumor behavior
questions.explanation: Passenger mutations accumulate but do not drive cancer phenotype.

questions.topic: Molecular Basis and Hallmarks of Cancer
questions.prompt: A core hallmark of cancer is:
options: Permanent dependence on normal growth control
questions.explanation: Cancer cells acquire autonomous growth signaling.

questions.topic: Molecular Basis and Hallmarks of Cancer
questions.prompt: Cancer cells evade growth suppression by altering:
questions.explanation: Loss of RB, TP53, and related pathways removes brakes on proliferation.

questions.topic: Molecular Basis and Hallmarks of Cancer
questions.prompt: Cancer cells acquire limitless replicative potential largely through:
questions.explanation: Telomere maintenance prevents senescence during repeated division.

questions.topic: Molecular Basis and Hallmarks of Cancer
questions.prompt: Angiogenesis helps tumors by:
options: Supplying nutrients and oxygen for expanding tumor mass
questions.answer: Supplying nutrients and oxygen for expanding tumor mass
questions.explanation: Tumors require new vessels beyond small diffusion-limited sizes.

questions.topic: Molecular Basis and Hallmarks of Cancer
questions.prompt: A tumor biopsy shows many mutations, but only a small subset repeatedly appears in independent samples and activates pathways controlling growth, survival, and invasion. The remaining mutations vary randomly between regions. Which term applies to the recurrent selected mutations?
questions.explanation: Driver mutations are selected because they contribute to malignant behavior.

questions.topic: Molecular Basis and Hallmarks of Cancer
questions.prompt: A cancer cell grows without exogenous growth factors, ignores antigrowth signals, resists apoptosis after DNA damage, induces blood vessels, and invades basement membrane. Which framework best integrates these diverse acquired properties?
questions.explanation: The hallmarks summarize acquired capabilities needed for malignant growth and spread.

questions.prompt: Tumor neoantigens are often generated by:
questions.explanation: Cancer mutations can create new peptides recognized by T cells.

questions.prompt: Aflatoxin B1 exposure in food leads to a characteristic TP53 mutation and greatly increases hepatocellular carcinoma risk, especially with hepatitis B infection. Which broad carcinogenic mechanism is most relevant?
options: Chemical carcinogenesis with mutational DNA damage
questions.answer: Chemical carcinogenesis with mutational DNA damage
questions.explanation: Aflatoxin is an indirect chemical carcinogen producing DNA adducts and TP53 mutations.

questions.prompt: The main antitumor effector lymphocyte is:
questions.explanation: CTLs recognize tumor peptides on MHC I and kill tumor cells.

questions.prompt: Immune checkpoint blockade commonly targets:
questions.explanation: Checkpoint inhibitors release brakes on antitumor T-cell responses.

questions.prompt: Tumors evade immunity by downregulating:
questions.explanation: Loss of MHC I impairs CD8 T-cell recognition.

questions.prompt: Chemical carcinogenesis typically includes:
questions.explanation: Initiation causes mutation; promotion drives clonal expansion.

questions.prompt: Direct-acting carcinogens require:
questions.explanation: Direct-acting agents are intrinsically carcinogenic.

questions.prompt: Indirect-acting chemical carcinogens are often activated by:
questions.explanation: Procarcinogens require metabolic conversion to ultimate carcinogens.

questions.prompt: A melanoma responds to anti-PD-1 therapy after biopsy shows many mutation-derived neoantigens and T cells at the tumor edge. The treatment does not kill tumor cells directly but restores exhausted T-cell activity. Which mechanism is being targeted?
questions.explanation: PD-1 blockade reinvigorates antitumor T-cell responses.

questions.prompt: A chemical produces no tumor by itself after a single exposure, but later application of a nonmutagenic irritant causes clonal expansion of initiated cells and papilloma formation. Which stage does the irritant represent?
questions.explanation: Promoters are nonmutagenic stimuli that expand initiated mutant clones.

questions.prompt: Metastasis means:
options: Spread of malignant tumor to distant sites
Replacement of one epithelium by another
questions.answer: Spread of malignant tumor to distant sites
questions.explanation: Metastasis is discontinuous spread of cancer.

questions.prompt: A renal cell carcinoma grows as a long tumor thrombus up the renal vein into the inferior vena cava, yet widespread metastases are initially absent. What concept from Robbins does this illustrate?
options: All venous invasion proves systemic spread
Intravascular extension can occur without immediate widespread metastasis
questions.answer: Intravascular extension can occur without immediate widespread metastasis
questions.explanation: Some tumors, especially renal cell carcinoma, show striking venous growth without parallel dissemination.

questions.prompt: Carcinomas most commonly spread initially by:
questions.explanation: Lymphatic spread is typical of carcinomas.

questions.prompt: Sarcomas more often spread by:
questions.explanation: Hematogenous spread is common in sarcomas.

questions.prompt: Loss of E-cadherin promotes invasion by reducing:
options: Tumor cell adhesion to neighboring epithelial cells
questions.answer: Tumor cell adhesion to neighboring epithelial cells
questions.explanation: Reduced adhesion permits dissociation and invasion.

questions.prompt: Matrix metalloproteinases help metastasis by:
options: Degrading extracellular matrix and basement membrane
questions.answer: Degrading extracellular matrix and basement membrane
questions.explanation: MMPs facilitate invasion through tissue barriers.

questions.prompt: Ovarian carcinoma commonly spreads by:
questions.explanation: Ovarian cancers often exfoliate cells into the peritoneal cavity.

questions.prompt: Portal venous drainage helps explain why colon carcinoma often metastasizes first to:
questions.explanation: Blood from colon drains through portal circulation to liver.

questions.prompt: A breast carcinoma loses E-cadherin expression, degrades basement membrane with proteases, migrates through stroma, enters lymphatics, and forms deposits in axillary nodes. Which step sequence best describes this event?
options: Local invasion followed by lymphatic metastasis
questions.answer: Local invasion followed by lymphatic metastasis
questions.explanation: Carcinoma metastasis requires invasion, intravasation, survival, extravasation, and colonization.

questions.prompt: A prostate carcinoma metastasizes to vertebral bodies despite other organs being closer in arterial flow. The spread follows valveless venous connections around the spine. Which pathway best explains this pattern?
questions.explanation: Pelvic tumors can spread to vertebrae through Batson paravertebral venous plexus.

questions.topic: Tumor Metabolism, Evasion of Death, Immortality, and Angiogenesis
questions.prompt: The Warburg effect refers to tumor cells using:
options: Anaerobic metabolism only when oxygen is absent
questions.explanation: Many cancers prefer glycolysis even in the presence of oxygen.

questions.topic: Tumor Metabolism, Evasion of Death, Immortality, and Angiogenesis
questions.prompt: A tumor expands beyond 1 to 2 mm and develops central hypoxia. HIF-1 alpha induces VEGF, leading to new but abnormal blood vessels that support further tumor growth and provide access to the circulation. Which process is central?
questions.explanation: Angiogenesis is required for growth beyond diffusion limits and aids dissemination.

questions.topic: Tumor Metabolism, Evasion of Death, Immortality, and Angiogenesis
questions.prompt: A major anti-apoptotic protein overexpressed in some lymphomas is:
questions.explanation: BCL2 blocks apoptosis and is activated in follicular lymphoma.

questions.topic: Tumor Metabolism, Evasion of Death, Immortality, and Angiogenesis
questions.prompt: VEGF primarily promotes:
questions.explanation: VEGF stimulates new vessel formation.

questions.topic: Tumor Metabolism, Evasion of Death, Immortality, and Angiogenesis
questions.prompt: Telomerase activation helps cancer cells by:
questions.explanation: Telomerase prevents telomere crisis and supports replicative immortality.

questions.topic: Tumor Metabolism, Evasion of Death, Immortality, and Angiogenesis
questions.prompt: Hypoxia increases angiogenesis mainly by stabilizing:
questions.explanation: HIF-1 alpha induces VEGF and metabolic adaptation under hypoxia.

questions.topic: Tumor Metabolism, Evasion of Death, Immortality, and Angiogenesis
questions.prompt: Follicular lymphoma commonly activates BCL2 through:
questions.explanation: The Ig heavy-chain enhancer drives BCL2 expression in t(14;18).

questions.topic: Tumor Metabolism, Evasion of Death, Immortality, and Angiogenesis
questions.prompt: Tumor angiogenesis often produces vessels that are:
questions.explanation: Tumor vessels are abnormal, tortuous, and permeable.

questions.topic: Tumor Metabolism, Evasion of Death, Immortality, and Angiogenesis
questions.prompt: A PET scan detects intense uptake of fluorodeoxyglucose in a lung cancer even though oxygen is available. The tumor diverts glycolytic intermediates into nucleotide, amino acid, and lipid synthesis. Which metabolic adaptation is being exploited?
questions.explanation: Aerobic glycolysis supports biosynthesis and is imaged by FDG-PET.

questions.topic: Tumor Metabolism, Evasion of Death, Immortality, and Angiogenesis
questions.prompt: A lymphoma cell survives despite signals that should trigger mitochondrial apoptosis. Cytogenetics shows t(14;18), placing BCL2 under immunoglobulin enhancer control. Which cancer hallmark is most directly promoted?
questions.explanation: BCL2 overexpression prevents apoptosis.

questions.prompt: A neoplasm is best defined as:
options: A clonal genetic disorder of cell growth with autonomous proliferation
A physiologic enlargement due only to increased workload
A reversible replacement of one mature cell type by another
A collection of neutrophils and necrotic debris
questions.answer: A clonal genetic disorder of cell growth with autonomous proliferation
questions.explanation: Modern pathology defines neoplasia as abnormal clonal growth driven by genetic or epigenetic alterations.

questions.prompt: A small, well-organized nodule of pancreatic tissue is found in the gastric submucosa during endoscopy. It is composed of normal pancreatic acini and ducts but is located in the wrong organ. Which term is most accurate?
questions.explanation: A choristoma is a heterotopic rest of normal tissue in an abnormal location.

questions.prompt: The tumor parenchyma is composed of:
questions.explanation: Parenchyma refers to the transformed cells that determine tumor behavior and nomenclature.

questions.prompt: The supportive non-neoplastic tissue of a tumor is called:
questions.explanation: Stroma includes connective tissue, blood vessels, and inflammatory cells that support tumor growth.

questions.prompt: A benign tumor of fibrous tissue is called a:
questions.explanation: Benign mesenchymal tumors often add -oma to the cell of origin.

questions.prompt: A malignant tumor arising from gland-forming epithelium is called:
questions.explanation: Malignant epithelial tumors are carcinomas; glandular differentiation makes them adenocarcinomas.

questions.prompt: A malignant tumor of mesenchymal origin is generally called a:
questions.explanation: Sarcomas arise from mesenchymal tissues such as muscle, bone, fat, and fibrous tissue.

questions.prompt: A teratoma contains:
options: Mature or immature tissues derived from more than one germ layer
Only misplaced normal tissue without neoplastic growth
questions.answer: Mature or immature tissues derived from more than one germ layer
questions.explanation: Teratomas arise from totipotent germ cells and may show multiple tissue types.

questions.prompt: An ovarian mass contains hair, sebaceous material, cartilage, and neural tissue arranged in a haphazard but mature fashion. The pathologist explains that the tumor arose from a totipotent germ cell. Which term best fits this lesion?
questions.explanation: Mature teratomas contain differentiated tissues from multiple germ layers, often in ovary.

questions.prompt: A lung nodule is made of disorganized but mature cartilage, bronchial epithelium, and connective tissue normally found in lung. Cytogenetic studies show a clonal abnormality, but the components are not foreign to the site. What is the best designation?
questions.explanation: Hamartomas are disorganized overgrowths of tissue native to the site and are often clonal benign lesions.

questions.prompt: Proto-oncogenes normally promote:
questions.explanation: Proto-oncogenes encode regulated proteins involved in growth signaling.

questions.prompt: A colon carcinoma has a KRAS mutation that locks RAS in its active GTP-bound state. Even if upstream EGFR is blocked, downstream signaling persists. Which concept explains resistance to anti-EGFR therapy?
questions.explanation: Activating KRAS mutations bypass upstream receptor blockade.

questions.prompt: An activated oncogene generally acts in a:
questions.explanation: One activated allele can drive growth.

questions.prompt: RAS is a:
questions.explanation: RAS transmits growth signals downstream of receptor tyrosine kinases.

questions.prompt: A common mechanism of MYC activation in Burkitt lymphoma is:
options: t(8;14) translocation near immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus
questions.answer: t(8;14) translocation near immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus
questions.explanation: Burkitt lymphoma often places MYC under Ig heavy-chain enhancer control.

questions.prompt: BCR-ABL in chronic myeloid leukemia encodes:
questions.explanation: The Philadelphia chromosome creates a fusion tyrosine kinase.

questions.prompt: HER2 amplification in breast cancer leads to:
questions.explanation: HER2 amplification drives growth signaling and is targetable.

questions.prompt: Cyclin D overexpression promotes cancer by:
questions.explanation: Cyclin D activates CDK4/6, phosphorylating RB and promoting S phase entry.

questions.prompt: A lung adenocarcinoma carries an EGFR kinase-domain mutation. The receptor signals without normal ligand regulation, activating downstream RAS and PI3K pathways. Which therapeutic principle follows from this molecular abnormality?
options: Use of targeted tyrosine kinase inhibition
questions.answer: Use of targeted tyrosine kinase inhibition
questions.explanation: Activated receptor tyrosine kinases may be blocked by specific kinase inhibitors.

questions.prompt: A leukemia cell contains t(9;22), producing a fusion protein that constitutively phosphorylates substrates and drives myeloid proliferation. The disease responds dramatically to imatinib. Which oncogenic mechanism is present?
questions.explanation: CML is driven by the BCR-ABL fusion kinase, targetable by imatinib.

questions.topic: Tumor Suppressor Genes and Cell-Cycle Control
questions.prompt: Tumor suppressor genes usually require:
options: Loss of both alleles for full inactivation
questions.answer: Loss of both alleles for full inactivation
questions.explanation: Most tumor suppressors follow the two-hit model.

questions.topic: Tumor Suppressor Genes and Cell-Cycle Control
questions.prompt: A tumor cell exposed to ionizing radiation fails to arrest the cell cycle, repair DNA, or undergo apoptosis. Sequencing shows biallelic TP53 loss. Which consequence best explains why this mutation accelerates cancer progression?
options: Survival and replication of genetically damaged cells
questions.answer: Survival and replication of genetically damaged cells
questions.explanation: Loss of p53 permits damaged cells to survive and accumulate additional mutations.

questions.topic: Tumor Suppressor Genes and Cell-Cycle Control
questions.prompt: RB normally controls transition from:
questions.explanation: RB restrains E2F and prevents S phase entry when hypophosphorylated.

questions.topic: Tumor Suppressor Genes and Cell-Cycle Control
questions.prompt: TP53 is often called the:
questions.explanation: p53 responds to DNA damage by inducing arrest, repair, senescence, or apoptosis.

questions.topic: Tumor Suppressor Genes and Cell-Cycle Control
questions.prompt: The two-hit hypothesis was first illustrated by:
questions.explanation: RB loss in hereditary and sporadic retinoblastoma illustrates two hits.

questions.topic: Tumor Suppressor Genes and Cell-Cycle Control
questions.prompt: APC mutation promotes colorectal carcinoma by activating:
questions.explanation: APC normally promotes beta-catenin degradation.

questions.topic: Tumor Suppressor Genes and Cell-Cycle Control
questions.prompt: Loss of E-cadherin is especially linked to:
options: Diffuse gastric carcinoma and lobular breast carcinoma
questions.answer: Diffuse gastric carcinoma and lobular breast carcinoma
questions.explanation: CDH1 loss reduces epithelial adhesion and promotes diffuse infiltrative growth.

questions.topic: Tumor Suppressor Genes and Cell-Cycle Control
questions.prompt: TGF-beta signaling normally acts as:
options: A growth-inhibitory pathway in many epithelial cells
questions.answer: A growth-inhibitory pathway in many epithelial cells
questions.explanation: Loss of TGF-beta pathway components removes growth suppression.

questions.topic: Tumor Suppressor Genes and Cell-Cycle Control
questions.prompt: A child inherits one mutant RB allele and develops bilateral retinoblastomas after somatic loss of the remaining normal allele in retinal cells. Years later, osteosarcoma risk is also increased. Which model explains this pattern?
options: Two-hit inactivation of a tumor suppressor gene
questions.answer: Two-hit inactivation of a tumor suppressor gene
questions.explanation: Inherited first hit plus somatic second hit produces early multiple tumors.

questions.topic: Tumor Suppressor Genes and Cell-Cycle Control
questions.prompt: A colon adenoma has APC loss, allowing beta-catenin to accumulate and enter the nucleus. The cell then transcribes growth-promoting genes despite absent WNT ligand. Which tumor suppressor pathway is disrupted?
questions.explanation: APC restrains WNT signaling by degrading beta-catenin.

questions.prompt: Staphylococcus aureus commonly causes:
questions.explanation: S. aureus is a classic pyogenic abscess-forming bacterium.

questions.prompt: A sexually active patient has purulent urethral discharge with intracellular gram-negative diplococci in neutrophils. The organism can vary pili and outer membrane proteins to evade immunity and reinfect hosts. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Gonorrhea shows gram-negative diplococci and antigenic variation.

questions.prompt: Streptococcus pyogenes is a:
questions.explanation: S. pyogenes is group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus.

questions.prompt: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a:
questions.explanation: Gonococcus is a gram-negative diplococcus.

questions.prompt: Diphtheria toxin inhibits:
questions.explanation: Corynebacterium diphtheriae toxin blocks elongation factor-2.

questions.prompt: Listeria monocytogenes is especially dangerous in:
options: Only patients with LDL receptor mutation
questions.explanation: Listeria causes severe disease in neonates, pregnant persons, elderly, and immunosuppressed.

questions.prompt: Pertussis is caused by:
questions.explanation: B. pertussis causes whooping cough.

questions.prompt: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is strongly associated with infections in:
options: Burn wounds and cystic fibrosis lungs
questions.answer: Burn wounds and cystic fibrosis lungs
questions.explanation: Pseudomonas thrives in moist environments and affects burns, devices, and CF airways.

questions.prompt: A burn patient develops a green-blue wound infection with sepsis. The organism is oxidase-positive, produces pigments, and often infects moist hospital environments and damaged tissue. Which bacterium is most likely?
questions.explanation: Pseudomonas causes burn wound infections with characteristic pigments and severe sepsis.

questions.prompt: A child with fever and sore throat develops a thick gray pharyngeal pseudomembrane that bleeds when scraped. The major systemic danger is myocarditis and neuropathy caused by toxin-mediated protein synthesis inhibition. Which pathogen is responsible?
questions.explanation: Diphtheria produces a pseudomembrane and toxin that inhibits EF-2.

questions.topic: Special Techniques and Diagnostic Approach to Infection
questions.prompt: Acid-fast stains are used mainly to detect:

questions.topic: Diet, Cancer Risk, and Trace Elements
questions.prompt: A population consuming mold-contaminated grains has high hepatocellular carcinoma rates, especially where hepatitis B is endemic. Tumors often contain a characteristic TP53 codon 249 mutation. Which dietary carcinogen is implicated?
questions.explanation: Aflatoxin B1 is a dietary hepatocarcinogen with a molecular TP53 signature.

questions.topic: Diet, Cancer Risk, and Trace Elements
questions.prompt: A child on a restricted artificial diet develops periorificial rash, diarrhea, alopecia, poor wound healing, depressed immunity, and impaired growth. The deficiency affects many enzymes, especially oxidases. Which trace element is lacking?
questions.explanation: Zinc deficiency causes acrodermatitis enteropathica-like lesions and immune/wound defects.

questions.prompt: Lead poisoning classically causes:
questions.explanation: Lead interferes with heme synthesis and causes basophilic stippling.

questions.prompt: A worker chronically exposed to arsenic develops hyperpigmentation, hyperkeratosis, peripheral neuropathy, and later skin and lung cancers. The toxin also interferes with mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. Which exposure best fits?
questions.explanation: Arsenic causes skin changes, neuropathy, mitochondrial toxicity, and cancer risk.

questions.prompt: Children with lead poisoning are especially prone to:
questions.explanation: Developing brains are highly vulnerable to lead.

questions.prompt: Mercury toxicity primarily injures:
questions.explanation: Mercury binds sulfhydryl groups and damages CNS and kidney.

questions.prompt: Lead inhibits heme synthesis by affecting:
questions.explanation: Lead blocks enzymes in heme synthesis.

questions.prompt: A classic adult neurologic manifestation of lead poisoning is:
options: Peripheral motor neuropathy with wrist drop
questions.answer: Peripheral motor neuropathy with wrist drop
questions.explanation: Adults often develop demyelinating peripheral neuropathy.

questions.prompt: Methylmercury exposure is most commonly from:
questions.explanation: Methylmercury bioaccumulates in aquatic food chains.

questions.prompt: Chronic arsenic exposure is linked to:
questions.explanation: Arsenic causes skin changes, neuropathy, and cancers.

questions.prompt: A toddler in an old house eats paint flakes and develops abdominal pain, irritability, developmental regression, microcytic anemia, and basophilic stippling. Wrist radiographs show dense metaphyseal lines. Which toxin is responsible?
questions.explanation: Lead exposure from old paint causes anemia, neurotoxicity, abdominal pain, and dense epiphyseal deposits.

questions.prompt: A pregnant patient eats contaminated fish with high methylmercury. The fetus later shows severe neurologic impairment with cerebral palsy, deafness, and blindness. Which disease pattern does Robbins associate with this exposure?
questions.explanation: Fetal mercury exposure can cause Minamata disease with severe CNS injury.

questions.prompt: Obesity is defined in adults by BMI greater than:
questions.explanation: BMI over 30 kg/m² is classified as obesity.

questions.prompt: A child with massive early-onset obesity has a mutation disabling the melanocortin-4 receptor pathway downstream of leptin-responsive hypothalamic neurons. Which regulatory system is primarily disrupted?
questions.explanation: MC4R participates in hypothalamic control of food intake and energy expenditure.

questions.prompt: Central obesity carries high risk because fat accumulates in:
questions.explanation: Visceral adiposity is metabolically harmful.

questions.prompt: Leptin is produced mainly by:
questions.explanation: Adipose tissue secretes leptin in proportion to fat stores.

questions.prompt: Leptin normally acts to:
options: Reduce appetite and increase energy expenditure
questions.answer: Reduce appetite and increase energy expenditure
questions.explanation: Leptin signals adequate fat stores to hypothalamic pathways.

questions.prompt: Common obesity often shows:
questions.explanation: Obese individuals often have high leptin but reduced response.

questions.prompt: Metabolic syndrome includes obesity with:
options: Insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and inflammation
questions.answer: Insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and inflammation
questions.explanation: Central obesity is linked to insulin resistance and proinflammatory metabolic disease.

questions.prompt: MC4R mutations are associated with:
questions.explanation: MC4R variants are among the more common monogenic obesity causes.

questions.prompt: A patient has central obesity, hypertension, hypertriglyceridemia, insulin resistance, and elevated CRP. Adipose tissue cytokines and lipid-induced inflammasome activation contribute to systemic inflammation. Which syndrome is best described?
questions.explanation: Metabolic syndrome links visceral obesity with insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and inflammation.

questions.prompt: An obese patient has high circulating leptin but persistent hyperphagia and low response to exogenous leptin. The problem is not absence of fat stores but impaired hypothalamic response to the signal. Which mechanism explains this?
questions.explanation: Most common obesity involves resistance to leptin signaling rather than leptin deficiency.

questions.prompt: Asbestos exposure is strongly associated with:
questions.explanation: Asbestos causes pulmonary fibrosis, lung carcinoma, and mesothelioma.

questions.prompt: A rubber industry worker chronically exposed to benzene develops marrow failure and later acute myeloid leukemia. The chemical is metabolized by hepatic CYP2E1 into toxic intermediates affecting progenitor cells. Which toxin is implicated?
questions.explanation: Benzene exposure is a classic occupational risk for leukemia.

questions.prompt: Benzene exposure increases risk of:
questions.explanation: Benzene metabolites injure marrow and increase leukemia risk.

questions.prompt: Nicotine is important in smoking because it is:
questions.explanation: Nicotine stimulates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and reinforces dependence.

questions.prompt: Smoking promotes emphysema partly by:
options: Recruiting leukocytes and increasing elastase-mediated lung injury
questions.answer: Recruiting leukocytes and increasing elastase-mediated lung injury
questions.explanation: Smoke induces inflammation and protease-antiprotease imbalance.

questions.prompt: Tobacco carcinogens include:
questions.explanation: These compounds form DNA adducts after metabolic activation.

questions.prompt: Smoking and asbestos together increase lung cancer risk because:
questions.explanation: Smoking greatly magnifies asbestos-related lung cancer risk.

questions.prompt: Occupational organic solvents can cause acute high-dose:
questions.explanation: Solvents such as chloroform and carbon tetrachloride can depress CNS and injure liver/kidney.

questions.prompt: A shipyard worker with decades of asbestos exposure develops progressive dyspnea, pleural plaques, and later malignant pleural mesothelioma. He also smokes heavily, increasing lung carcinoma risk. Which occupational agent is central?
questions.explanation: Asbestos causes plaques, asbestosis, lung carcinoma, and mesothelioma.

questions.prompt: A smoker’s lung cancer genome contains thousands of mutations with signatures typical of tobacco carcinogens. CYP metabolism generated electrophilic intermediates that formed DNA adducts repaired by error-prone pathways. Which exposure is most responsible?
options: Cigarette smoke polycyclic hydrocarbons and nitrosamines
questions.answer: Cigarette smoke polycyclic hydrocarbons and nitrosamines
questions.explanation: Tobacco carcinogens produce DNA adducts and characteristic mutational signatures.

questions.prompt: Marasmus is primarily due to deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Marasmus is overall calorie deprivation with wasting.

questions.prompt: A young woman with binge eating and self-induced vomiting develops parotid enlargement, enamel erosion, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, and normal-to-low body weight. Which nutritional/behavioral disorder best explains these findings?
questions.explanation: Bulimia involves binge-purge behavior with characteristic dental and electrolyte effects.

questions.prompt: Kwashiorkor is primarily associated with:
questions.explanation: Kwashiorkor features hypoalbuminemia and edema.

questions.prompt: Anorexia nervosa is characterized by:
options: Self-induced starvation and distorted body image
questions.answer: Self-induced starvation and distorted body image
questions.explanation: Anorexia involves psychiatric restriction of intake and severe undernutrition.

questions.prompt: Edema in kwashiorkor is mainly due to:
questions.explanation: Low plasma oncotic pressure from protein deficiency causes edema.

questions.prompt: Marasmus typically shows:
options: Moon face and fatty liver only
Severe muscle wasting without prominent edema
questions.answer: Severe muscle wasting without prominent edema
questions.explanation: Marasmus is cachectic wasting with relative preservation of serum protein until late.

questions.prompt: Fatty liver in kwashiorkor is caused partly by:
questions.explanation: Protein deficiency impairs lipoprotein export from liver.

questions.prompt: Bulimia nervosa commonly causes:
options: Dental enamel erosion and electrolyte abnormalities
questions.answer: Dental enamel erosion and electrolyte abnormalities
questions.explanation: Vomiting exposes teeth to acid and can cause hypokalemic alkalosis.

questions.prompt: A severely malnourished child has marked wasting, loss of subcutaneous fat, growth retardation, and no significant edema. Serum albumin is relatively preserved compared with a child who has flaky paint dermatosis and fatty liver. Which condition is present?
questions.explanation: Marasmus is total calorie deprivation with severe wasting but less edema than kwashiorkor.

questions.prompt: A child weaned onto a carbohydrate-rich but protein-poor diet develops edema, distended abdomen, flaky skin lesions, hair color changes, and fatty liver. The edema reflects low plasma oncotic pressure. Which diagnosis fits?
questions.explanation: Kwashiorkor is protein malnutrition with hypoalbuminemia, edema, dermatosis, and fatty liver.

questions.prompt: Vitamin A deficiency causes:
questions.explanation: Vitamin A is required for vision and epithelial maintenance.

questions.prompt: A malnourished alcoholic develops confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia, then memory loss and confabulation. The disorder reflects impaired carbohydrate metabolism in vulnerable brain regions. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely?
questions.explanation: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is due to thiamine deficiency.

questions.prompt: Vitamin D deficiency in children causes:
questions.explanation: Defective mineralization of growing bone causes rickets.

questions.prompt: Vitamin C deficiency causes:
questions.explanation: Vitamin C deficiency impairs collagen hydroxylation.

questions.prompt: Thiamine deficiency causes:
questions.explanation: Vitamin B1 deficiency injures heart and nervous system.

questions.prompt: Niacin deficiency causes:
questions.explanation: Pellagra is the three Ds, and may progress to death.

questions.prompt: Vitamin K deficiency causes:
questions.explanation: Vitamin K is needed for factors II, VII, IX, and X.

questions.prompt: Vitamin A toxicity may cause:
options: Liver injury and increased intracranial pressure
questions.answer: Liver injury and increased intracranial pressure
questions.explanation: Hypervitaminosis A can be hepatotoxic and teratogenic.

questions.prompt: A child with limited sunlight exposure develops bowed legs and widened growth plates. Serum calcium is maintained by elevated PTH, but phosphate remains low, impairing mineralization of osteoid and epiphyseal cartilage. Which deficiency is responsible?
questions.explanation: Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets through defective mineralization.

questions.prompt: A sailor on a long voyage develops swollen bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, poor wound healing, and fragile blood vessels. The molecular defect is impaired hydroxylation of proline and lysine in procollagen. Which vitamin is deficient?
questions.explanation: Scurvy reflects defective collagen synthesis from vitamin C deficiency.

questions.prompt: A xenobiotic is:
options: A foreign chemical substance in the body
questions.answer: A foreign chemical substance in the body
questions.explanation: Xenobiotics include drugs, pollutants, and industrial chemicals.

questions.prompt: Carbon tetrachloride causes hepatic injury after conversion to a trichloromethyl free radical in the endoplasmic reticulum. Lipid peroxidation then damages membranes. Which cellular injury mechanism is central?
options: Free radical generation during xenobiotic metabolism
questions.answer: Free radical generation during xenobiotic metabolism
questions.explanation: CYP-mediated metabolism can generate free radicals that injure membranes.

questions.prompt: The major phase I xenobiotic enzyme system is:
questions.explanation: CYP enzymes catalyze oxidation, reduction, and hydrolysis reactions.

questions.prompt: Phase II metabolism generally makes compounds:
questions.explanation: Conjugation reactions increase excretion in urine or bile.

questions.prompt: Phase I reactions include:
questions.explanation: Phase I modifies chemicals through oxidation/reduction/hydrolysis.

questions.prompt: Phase II reactions include:
options: Glucuronidation, sulfation, methylation, and glutathione conjugation
questions.answer: Glucuronidation, sulfation, methylation, and glutathione conjugation
questions.explanation: Phase II conjugates metabolites to increase water solubility.

questions.prompt: Xenobiotic metabolism can increase toxicity when it:
questions.explanation: Some CYP products are electrophilic or free radical intermediates that injure cells.

questions.prompt: Genetic polymorphisms in CYP enzymes can alter:
questions.explanation: CYP variation changes metabolism rates and toxic metabolite production.

questions.prompt: A chemical is harmless until hepatic CYP enzymes convert it to a reactive intermediate that binds DNA and creates mutations. Phase II conjugation is overwhelmed, and long-term cancer risk rises. Which principle is illustrated?
questions.explanation: Some xenobiotics become toxic only after phase I activation.

questions.prompt: A patient taking multiple drugs develops toxicity after a second medication induces CYP activity. The same dose now generates more reactive metabolite and oxidative stress. Which feature explains the altered response?
options: Inducible and variable cytochrome P-450 metabolism
questions.answer: Inducible and variable cytochrome P-450 metabolism
questions.explanation: CYP activity varies with genetics and exposure to inducers or inhibitors.

questions.prompt: A patient with plaque psoriasis improves with topical calcipotriene. The mechanism is:
options: Vitamin D receptor activation normalizing keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation
questions.answer: Vitamin D receptor activation normalizing keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation
questions.explanation: Vitamin D analogs regulate epidermal growth and immune activity in psoriasis.

questions.prompt: High-potency topical corticosteroids improve eczema because they:
questions.explanation: Topical glucocorticoids reduce cytokines, vasodilation, and immune cell activity.

questions.prompt: A patient using clobetasol on the face develops skin thinning and telangiectasias. This is due to:
questions.explanation: Potent topical steroids can cause atrophy, striae, telangiectasias, and perioral dermatitis.

questions.prompt: Tacrolimus ointment is useful for atopic dermatitis on thin skin because it:
options: Inhibits calcineurin without causing steroid atrophy
questions.answer: Inhibits calcineurin without causing steroid atrophy
questions.explanation: Topical calcineurin inhibitors reduce T-cell cytokine signaling and avoid steroid skin thinning.

questions.prompt: Topical benzoyl peroxide helps acne partly by:
options: Generating free radicals toxic to Cutibacterium acnes
questions.answer: Generating free radicals toxic to Cutibacterium acnes
questions.explanation: Benzoyl peroxide is antibacterial and comedolytic and does not cause bacterial resistance alone.

questions.prompt: Isotretinoin is highly effective for severe nodulocystic acne because it:
options: Shrinks sebaceous glands and reduces sebum production
questions.answer: Shrinks sebaceous glands and reduces sebum production
questions.explanation: Systemic retinoids target sebaceous gland activity, comedogenesis, and inflammation.

questions.prompt: A woman starting isotretinoin must use strict pregnancy prevention because it is:
questions.explanation: Isotretinoin can cause severe birth defects and requires pregnancy prevention programs.

questions.prompt: Terbinafine treats tinea corporis by inhibiting:
questions.explanation: Terbinafine blocks ergosterol synthesis and accumulates in keratinized tissue.

questions.prompt: Permethrin treats scabies because it:
questions.explanation: Permethrin is a pyrethroid neurotoxin for mites and lice with low mammalian toxicity when used properly.

questions.prompt: Topical minoxidil promotes hair growth most plausibly by:
options: Shortening telogen and prolonging anagen through follicular vascular/signaling effects
questions.answer: Shortening telogen and prolonging anagen through follicular vascular/signaling effects
questions.explanation: Minoxidil promotes hair growth through follicular effects; irritation and unwanted hair growth can occur.

questions.prompt: A child with abdominal pain, anemia, and developmental delay has elevated lead level. Chelation with succimer is useful because it:
options: Binds lead and increases urinary excretion
questions.answer: Binds lead and increases urinary excretion
questions.explanation: Succimer is an oral chelator used for lead poisoning in appropriate cases.

questions.prompt: Lead poisoning causes microcytic anemia partly by inhibiting:
questions.explanation: Lead disrupts heme synthesis enzymes, producing anemia and basophilic stippling.

questions.prompt: A patient with severe arsenic or mercury poisoning may be treated with dimercaprol because it:
options: Provides sulfhydryl groups that bind heavy metals
questions.answer: Provides sulfhydryl groups that bind heavy metals
questions.explanation: Dimercaprol chelates certain heavy metals through thiol binding.

questions.prompt: Iron overdose with vomiting, metabolic acidosis, and shock is treated with:
questions.explanation: Deferoxamine chelates iron and is used in severe iron poisoning.

questions.prompt: A patient exposed to carbon monoxide has normal PaO2 but low oxygen content. Hyperbaric oxygen helps by:
options: Accelerating dissociation of CO from hemoglobin and improving tissue oxygen delivery
questions.answer: Accelerating dissociation of CO from hemoglobin and improving tissue oxygen delivery
questions.explanation: CO binds hemoglobin with high affinity and impairs oxygen delivery; oxygen shortens carboxyhemoglobin half-life.

questions.prompt: Cyanide poisoning after smoke inhalation causes lactic acidosis because cyanide:
questions.explanation: Cyanide prevents cellular oxygen utilization, causing histotoxic hypoxia and lactic acidosis.

questions.prompt: Hydroxocobalamin treats cyanide poisoning by:
questions.explanation: Hydroxocobalamin scavenges cyanide and is commonly used in smoke-inhalation cyanide toxicity.

questions.prompt: Organophosphate poisoning with salivation, bronchorrhea, fasciculations, and miosis requires atropine plus pralidoxime because:
options: Atropine blocks muscarinic effects while pralidoxime can reactivate acetylcholinesterase before aging
Atropine reactivates AChE and pralidoxime dries secretions
questions.answer: Atropine blocks muscarinic effects while pralidoxime can reactivate acetylcholinesterase before aging
questions.explanation: Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase; treatment addresses muscarinic crisis and enzyme reactivation.

questions.prompt: Nitrate-contaminated well water can cause infant cyanosis because nitrates produce:
questions.explanation: Nitrates oxidize hemoglobin iron, impairing oxygen delivery; infants are vulnerable.

questions.prompt: Methylene blue treats significant methemoglobinemia by:
options: Reducing ferric iron in hemoglobin back to ferrous iron
questions.answer: Reducing ferric iron in hemoglobin back to ferrous iron
questions.explanation: Methylene blue accelerates reduction of methemoglobin via NADPH-dependent pathways; caution is needed in G6PD deficiency.

questions.prompt: A patient with open-angle glaucoma is started on latanoprost at night. The main pressure-lowering mechanism is:
options: Reduced aqueous production by beta blockade
questions.explanation: Prostaglandin analogs increase uveoscleral outflow and are common first-line glaucoma therapy.

questions.prompt: A patient using latanoprost notices darker irides and longer eyelashes. This adverse effect is due to:
options: Prostaglandin receptor effects on melanocytes and hair follicles
questions.answer: Prostaglandin receptor effects on melanocytes and hair follicles
questions.explanation: Prostaglandin analogs can cause iris pigmentation, eyelash growth, and periocular changes.

questions.prompt: Timolol eye drops lower intraocular pressure by:
questions.explanation: Topical beta blockers reduce ciliary body aqueous humor production.

questions.prompt: A patient with asthma becomes short of breath after timolol eye drops. The reason is:
questions.explanation: Even topical ophthalmic beta blockers can be systemically absorbed and provoke bronchospasm.

questions.prompt: Dorzolamide helps glaucoma because it inhibits:
options: Carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary body
questions.answer: Carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary body
questions.explanation: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors reduce bicarbonate-dependent aqueous humor secretion.

questions.prompt: Acetazolamide is used acutely for high intraocular pressure but can cause:
questions.explanation: Systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibition causes bicarbonaturia, acidosis, and electrolyte effects.

questions.prompt: Pilocarpine can open the trabecular meshwork in angle-closure glaucoma by:
options: Contracting ciliary muscle and producing miosis
questions.answer: Contracting ciliary muscle and producing miosis
questions.explanation: Muscarinic agonists constrict the pupil and contract ciliary muscle, improving trabecular outflow.

questions.prompt: Apraclonidine lowers intraocular pressure after laser procedures mainly through:
questions.explanation: Topical alpha-2 agonists reduce aqueous humor production and may increase outflow.

questions.prompt: Intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy for wet macular degeneration works by:
options: Reducing pathologic choroidal neovascularization and leakage
questions.answer: Reducing pathologic choroidal neovascularization and leakage
questions.explanation: VEGF drives abnormal vessel growth and leakage in neovascular AMD.

questions.prompt: Topical tropicamide is used for fundus examination because it:
options: Blocks muscarinic receptors causing mydriasis and cycloplegia
questions.answer: Blocks muscarinic receptors causing mydriasis and cycloplegia
questions.explanation: Antimuscarinics dilate the pupil and paralyze accommodation.
